speakeroldname: Hon. William Rompkey (Grand Falls-White Bay- Labrador) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-YOUTH-EDUCATION AND EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
That this House condemns the Government for its abandonment of our youth and its failure to provide adequate support for their education and training or meaningful employment and job opportunities, both temporary and permanent.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the motion before us concerns one of the most important, if not the most important, groups in our society today.
Let me begin by reading from the report of the Senate committee chaired by the Hon. Jacques Hebert who is well known in this Parliament and in the country for his concern for young people. The report of the Senate states:
The public hearings proved to be a disturbing experience for the committee members, as we were not only confronted with distressing facts and statistics, but also actually met the young Canadians grappling with complicated problems. It would not be an exaggeration to say that by the time the hearings ended, the attitudes of the Committee members had changed. We had realized that the situation for a great number of young people is intolerable and that we must convince the public of this.
Hence, this motion today. Sometimes we talk blithely about young people, about our children and our grandchildren.
Obviously there is an intrinsic worth for the young people in our society. We love them because they are ours and we want to see them have the best possible world.
However, another point must be made. It is that at this stage of Canada's life they have more than simply an intrinsic value to us as young people because Canada is moving from one kind of society to another. With the exception of parts of Ontario and Quebec, Canada has been a resource-based society. We have been harvesting the sea, harvesting the forests and the minerals from our soils, and transporting them sometimes in a raw state and sometimes in a manufactured state.
However, the day when Canada can depend on shipping out raw resources is fast coming to an end. The easy times are over for us in Canada and the tough times are ahead.
We are moving from a resource-based and manufacturing economy to an information economy and an information age in which we will have to depend more than ever on our young people.
While they have an intrinsic value for us, in the information economy toward which we are moving they will be much more important to us in the future.
Let us consider the statistics arising from the Senate report and other research into the state of young people in this country today. Young people are important to the future of Canada, yet 48 per cent of single people under the age of 25 in Canada today live below the poverty line. There are 100,000 young people with children who are living below the poverty line.
Youth unemployment in my Province of Newfoundland is 32 per cent; in Nova Scotia it is 23 per cent; in British Columbia it is 23 per cent; and the unemployment rate for young people in Alberta is 2.5 times what it was in 1980. Last year in Canada only 170,000 students could find summer jobs.
In order to go beyond those statistics and understand the distress that exists with our young people, one only need look at the enormous jump in suicides and attempted suicides among young people in the past number of years to realize that this problem is serious. In 1961, for example, the suicide rate among males between the ages of 20 and 24 was 9 per 100,000. In 1985, it was 30 per 100,000, which is more than three times the level of 1961.
I do not lay these statistics on the table as scare tactics or for rhetorical purposes, but to illustrate graphically that this problem is serious. It requires serious solutions, but what has been done?
It is true that all of this cannot be blamed on the present Government because no one is naive enough to think that this suddenly began in 1984. Certainly, however, the Government has a responsibility to bring in programs that will address this situation. Let us consider what the Government has done. Student debt loads from Newfoundland to British Columbia range from $14,000 to $24,000 upon graduation. Canadian students who depend upon the Canada Student Loans Program and the various provincial loan programs which complement it have debt loads of between $14,000 and $20,000 when they graduate. These young people have less ability to find jobs. They are growing in numbers and experiencing the kind of despair which I just described. It is completely unacceptable.
I say to the Government that the first thing we need is a complete overhaul of the Canada Student Loans Program. Instead of loading a debt burden upon the present generation, who cannot and should not have to bear the burden, we should
May 7, 1987

be moving toward a bursary program. We should be investing in young people instead of loading debt upon their shoulders. We should be injecting money into the system so that they can make a contribution.
Student access is being limited in our universities. We are in danger of becoming a society which offers education to an elite group. There are more and more students in low income brackets who cannot afford and therefore do not have access to colleges and universities. There is a great danger in Canada today that we are offering the services of those institutions only to the elite.
What we have seen consistently over the past few years, in particular, has been a retrenchment in the funds offered for the support of universities and colleges. I am talking particularly about the Established Programs Financing which the Government-and we must lay it directly at its door-has deliberately and knowingly cut back.
I should like to refer to the background of this matter. There was to have been an 8 per cent increase in Established Programs Financing to the provinces. It was an agreement between the federal Government and the provincial Governments. The agreement was unilaterally abrogated by the Government of Canada. Instead, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced that there would be an increase of only 6 per cent.
What did it mean? It meant that somehow the provinces had to come up with the shortfall from their own funds. Can one imagine the Province of Newfoundland-and the Premier himself has admitted that it is on the verge of bankruptcy- finding close to an extra $200 million out of its own pocket? Can one imagine it digging down deep into its pocket to find money by 1990 which it does not have in order to make up for the shortfall in Established Programs Financing?
This means that the universities get less money and that post-secondary institutions have less money with which to operate. As a result, what do they do? The only thing available to them is tuition fees. Thus they start raising tuition fees to try to carry on their programs.
What does that mean? It means that only those people who can afford to pay get in. This is what I mean by saying that the policies of the Government are forcing upon the universities and colleges a process whereby we in Canada are becoming a group which offers education only to the elite.
Student access has a second difficulty. The students may try to find some other way of supplementing their income to help put themselves through university. One way of doing it of course is by having a job in the summer-time. However, fewer and fewer students are able to find summer jobs. This is in addition to their Canada student loans, which amount to an unbearable debt load, the tuition they are required to pay and inadequate housing.
We found that all across the country too few students had access to adequate housing, again because the universities and
Supply
colleges did not have the budgets and no one else was building that housing.
Students, in their attempt to attain their own resources, always depend upon summer jobs. However, what has happened to summer jobs? They have been cut back.
Last year there were adequate funds under the Canadian Jobs Strategy, but this year there has been a 15 per cent decrease. The Government of Canada says that that is mainly because it cut out the census. However, it does not matter from where the money comes or to what the money is applied. A job is a job is a job. If we take away $30 million or 15 per cent from last year's program, it means that many fewer young people in Canada have access to summer jobs. I do not care whether it was for the census or whatever; the fact is that less money is available for young people to find summer jobs this year than there was last year, and the Government must answer for it.
The change in the Canadian Jobs Strategy has also created difficulties for community colleges. The private sector is now given priority in the use of funds under the Canadian Jobs Strategy. Across the country from Newfoundland to British Columbia community colleges and CEGEPs have less funds available to them now than they had in the past. For example, we were told by Algonquin College in Ottawa that it received about 50 per cent of the funds than it received last year. Why is this? It is because funds were offered to the private sector.
What did the private sector do? It said that it did not want to do training because it was not very good at it, and returned the funds. As far as I know, many of them were unused. The story we heard from institutions such as Algonquin and the British Columbia Institute of Technology was that they had available to them a little more than 50 per cent of what they had in the past, because of the emphasis on the private sector under the Canadian Jobs Strategy. This is something which the Government must address if it is to provide proper consideration for the funding of our post-secondary institutions.
The closing of student employment centres is also a backward step. I call upon the Government to reinstate them.
My colleague in the Senate, Senator Fairbairn, recently highlighted for us in a very dramatic and effective way another serious problem, that is, the problem of illiteracy. We must remember that we are talking about a society which is moving from a resource-based economy to an information economy; we must always bear that in mind. We are talking about a fundamental change in society. Yet, when we need people who can think better and think smarter than ever before, what do we have? We have one million adult Canadians who cannot read or write at all and four million more who cannot read or write well enough to function adequately in society. Senator Fairbairn referred to them as "our country's hidden shame", and she was right; she put her finger on it.
I see the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie) across the way. I know he is working on a program. I count upon him as a

May 7, 1987
Supply
gentleman and a politician with a distinguished record to develop a program which will address the problem. As I said, I know he is working on it, and I wish him well. However, I wanted to highlight the issue today as a serious problem.
For example, my own province has the highest illiteracy rate anywhere in Canada. Over 30 per cent of Newfoundlanders over the age of 15 years have less than grade 9 education, and the national figure is 22 per cent. We need a national program to address this serious national problem.
It is not enough, in any of these things, to say that education is a provincial responsibility. It is true, but it does not solve the problem. As the country moves into a new kind of society, we need a national policy to address a serious national problem. I call upon the Government to take the matter very seriously. The tide must be turned.
We must increase the funding we make available to our universities and colleges for research as well. The irony is that Dr. John Polanyi, after he received the Nobel Prize, advised Canadian students and researchers who wanted to follow a career which could come anywhere close to resembling his to move to the United States. What a shocking indictment of the research capabilities of Canadian institutions!
The first thing we need is an increase in funding to universities and colleges, not simply for core programs but for research capabilities as well. Second, we need a fundamental change in the Canada Student Loans Program that will stress not debt loads but an investment in young Canadians and a move from a loan program to a bursary program. Third, we need the reinstatement of the First Chance Program for young people, a guarantee that when young people finish their training and education, they will have available to them, at least in the beginning, a job.
We cannot guarantee them a job for life and no one should be guaranteed a job for life. Every person is independent and has the right to make his own way in this world. However, in the kind of society into which we are moving, I believe we have to bring education beyond simply grade 13 or a Bachelor's degree. I believe we have to tell people that we will start them off and given them the first chance in the market-place. We have to provide adequate funding for summer jobs and we have to have a national program for attack on what Senator Fairbairn called this country's hidden shame, and that is, the problem of illiteracy in Canada. Those are the things that must be done. We on this side call upon the Government to take this matter seriously and to address these very serious problems.
If I may, I would like to conclude by reading from the Senate report on youth. Its concluding paragraphs read as follows:
Our society appears only too happy that today's youth seem to have an infinite
amount of patience and are less demanding than previous generations. But
how long will their patience hold out? In other industrialized countries, it
seems to have been stretched to the limit. In fact, in several regions of Europe, patience has given way to exasperation and violence.
What we are seeing on Canadian campuses today is the beginning of the re-enactment of the spirit of the sixties. Bob Dylan, where are you? Perhaps Bruce Springsteen, I do not know, will be the new symbol of the eighties. I believe we are starting to see a regeneration of that kind of spirit on campuses now. The report continues:
Despite the economic recession from which we have barely recovered, Canada is one of the richest countries in the world. We have at our disposal the means by which to help our young people. The public and political will to remedy the situation must be displayed without further delay. Each Canadian community must assume control of its own affairs and put its imagination to work so that we may improve the present and future lives of our young people. Just as in the event of a major national disaster, we as Canadians must concentrate all our energy to solve this serious problem.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-YOUTH-EDUCATION AND EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
First, Mr. Speaker, I wish to greet you personally.
From the outset I should like to commend my colleague for a speech whose tone was particularly appropriate to the topic and tell him that I am pleasantly surprised at the approach he took today. Quite frankly I was expecting something else, more like much more partisan remarks on the part of my colleague opposite. I should like to emphasize how grateful I am that he took such a constructive approach.
I should like to say that the issue covers a lot of ground, that in all likelihood we agree with most of what he has brought to our attention today. He pinpoints problems which every one of us has acknowledged as having become ever more significant in recent years. Mr. Speaker, this is why I want to stress the fact that my colleague has raised problems which the Government is likely prepared to view as being identified.
I have two brief questions for him.
First, I should like to ask him what is the position of the Liberal Party of Canada with respect to what they consider to be the most urgent issue now facing young Canadians. He did refer to some of them but I was unable to find in his remarks a clear indication of what the most important problem might be.
Second, perhaps he might tell me who should be included in the eventual quest for solutions to what the Liberal Party of Canada deems to be the most important problem, or again the five points he mentioned in his speech?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-YOUTH-EDUCATION AND EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is very difficult to highlight one particular problem that needs attention because I think that would be over-simplifying what is a complex problem. I would suggest to the Minister what he could do if he wanted to help those who are in the middle of their education and training now. I am not talking about those who are coming into the educational system or those who have gone through it and are still experiencing despair and disillusionment in their difficulty in finding job opportunities because job opportunities are something the Government can and should create for those people. However, if he wanted to help those who are in the
May 7, 1987

middle of their education now, he could deal with what I think is the top priority for Canadian students.
If members of the Canadian Federation of Students were here in this Chamber today, I think they would tell us to change the Canada Student Loans Program so that students will not have to bear that excessive debt burden of between $14,000 and $20,000 on graduation. Basically, we should change the Canada Student Loans Program from a loan program to a bursary program. I think that is what they would ask and that is what I ask on their behalf today.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-YOUTH-EDUCATION AND EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask my hon. friend a question about his very excellent speech which outlined the nature of the problems facing students. One thing I thought was missing from the Hon. Member's speech was any identification of what the Government has done to solve the problems.
I as well as other Hon. Members have looked high and low through all of the brochures and files and the only thing I could come up with was Hot-100. I gave this booklet to my teenage son the other day so he could look through it and evaluate it because he is the person for whom it was designed. To summarize my son Nils' comment, he said: "Dad, I looked through this and I couldn't find anything in here that was of direct relevance to me as a 17-year-old boy.
Has the Hon. Member looked through Hot-1001 What is his view of this initiative which I suppose is the only one the Government has taken in the last two and a half years?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-YOUTH-EDUCATION AND EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is a question that is best addressed and will be addressed to the Minister when he speaks. It will be for him to put on the record what the Government has done or has not done.
Today's motion clearly indicates that this is a serious national problem which requires a serious national response and, in answer to the Hon. Member, so far we have not seen a serious, co-ordinated, comprehensive response from the Government on how it will deal with the problem of youth in Canada in the 1980s. I look forward to the speech of the Minister. Perhaps he can build on the booklet about which we have just been told and tell us exactly what the Government intends to do to address the problems we have identified today.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-YOUTH-EDUCATION AND EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to refer to the reference that was made to members of the Liberal Party preferring a bursary program to the present loan program. That is precisely what the Liberal Party proposed the second to last time it was in opposition under the leadership of Mr. Pearson. He went to the young people of Canada in the early 1960s offering a program of 10,000 scholarships. Once elected, the Government did not deliver the 10,000 scholarships. It delivered the loan program, which it now does not want. The loan program we have was initiated under the federal leadership of the Liberal Party with the co-operation of the various provinces.
Supply
The point I would like to make for the record is simply that I take it that the Liberal Opposition is now reverting to the position it held when it was in opposition previously. The fact that it did not deliver on that proposal when it became a Government, may suggest something about the credibility of its policy now.
There was another point made about not providing any job opportunities for young people. Statistics indicate that since 1984 not only has the total of new job opportunities increased dramatically but it has increased for young people. Tragically, the problem of unemployment remains largely a regional problem, and that is really what we should be addressing, not young people across the country, but rather how we can create greater job opportunities for all people in those areas which have not been able to come abreast of other parts of the country.
I would just like to throw one point into the discussion, and I hope some future speaker who has adequate time will take it up, that is, the quality of education and training in Canada should have a priority. If this country is to compete successfully throughout the balance of this century and into the 21st century, it is going to have to compete with a world which is increasingly better educated and equipped. We should be addressing ourselves to the challenge.
How can 25 million people, trying to live and function in the second largest country in the world use its resources, which are always limited however rich they are, to the best advantage? How can they most effectively be used to provide the training, research and development opportunities for young people which will enable them to compete effectively with the rest of the world?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, I want to congratulate my hon. friend and colleague, the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey), for providing us with this opportunity today to discuss what has to be one of the most critical issues facing the country. That, of course, is the future of our young people.
I am pleased to respond to the motion of the Hon. Member which reads:
That this House condemns the Government for its abandonment of our youth
and its failure to provide adequate support for their education and training or
meaningful employment and job opportunities, both temporary and
permanent.
I want to begin my remarks by saying that I, like the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador, feel that the Government has in a sense turned its back on young people. I do not understand why it has done that. I want to spend a few moments explaining why I feel the Government has abandoned the young people and why it has failed to provided adequate financial support to develop their educational careers and their family futures.
In the last few weeks I have been touring the high schools in my constituency as well as junior high schools and elementary schools. I have talked to our young people, particularly those in graduating classes. There are hundreds of thousands of young people who are about to leave secondary school to begin their careers in post-secondary education and training. One common theme I have noticed in discussions with individuals and classes of young people is a growing sense of disillusionment and frustration about the fact that their future appears to be very uncertain. There is a fuzziness in terms of where the country is going, what opportunities there are for the future.
When most of us in the House of Commons graduated from high school or post-secondary institutions we had perhaps half a dozen jobs from which to choose. Now there are half a dozen young people competing for the one job available. That becomes woefully obvious when you look at the unemployment figures for young people. Today 500,000 young Canadians fall into the category of the unemployed. This does not include the
20.000	or 30,000 young people who have given up and are not now actively looking for work. They come from communities where the unemployment rate is from 30 per cent to 50 per cent. There is simply no point in going up and down the streets looking for work in an area where the unemployment level is so unbelievably high.
Those figures totally ignore native young people who are not factored into the formal statistics at all. In addition, there are
180.000	young people who have to be described as severely
May 7, 1987

underemployed. They may work for five hours a week at McDonald's or 15 hours a week in a part-time job with no security and no prospects for permanency.
Therefore, the actual unemployment rate for people between the ages of 15 and 24 is 23 per cent to 25 per cent. In other words, almost one-quarter of the young people of Canada are in an almost hopeless situation at the time of life when they ought to be developing themselves creatively and positively. They should be developing careers and starting families. Twenty-five per cent of young Canadian people are, for all intents and purposes, jobless. That is virtually an immoral situation. We should be spending day after day in the House of Commons searching for solutions to this national catastrophe. I think we would all agree that this is a serious crisis situation.
Yet it is the Opposition which calls for a debate to seek solutions for this. It is not the Government or the Minister of State for Youth (Mr. Charest) but the Opposition which calls for a special debate to address the plight of young people. That does not bode well in terms of how serious the Government is on this issue. If the Government were serious on this issue it would be doing something.
To be fair, I have to admit that the Government has done something. For example, it eliminated the Katimavik program and promised a new youth program in February of last year. That promise has not yet been kept. The budget for the youth Ministry was totally eliminated. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) slowed the rate of growth of transfer payments, which will result in the loss of $1.5 billion between 1986 and 1991 in post-secondary education. Funds for the International Year of Youth were eliminated and no new funds were allocated to continue this important work.
Yesterday in the House of Commons the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) mentioned Challenge '85, '86 and '87. He said that Challenge '85 created 100,000 jobs. One would assume that in 1986 when the unemployment situation was worsening the program would create more jobs. However, the Deputy Prime Minister said that Challenge '86 created only 93,000 jobs. He went on to say that the funding for Challenge '87 will remain the same as last year, which is obviously woefully inadequate. As my friend, the Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey), indicated, not only is it inadequate, it is a move to facilitate jobs in the private sector. Although we applaud this, it is at the expense of jobs in the public sector. Non-profit organizations could put young people to work in meaningful ways for the summer.
I have experienced, as I am sure all other Members of Parliament have, the frustration of collecting hundreds and hundreds of Challenge '87 job applications, only to have half of them tossed out because there is no money and to have requests for 10 or 15 young people cut down to three or four young people. It tears my heart out to know that the one program which the federal Government has to assist young people during the summer, which is good as far as it goes, is so
Supply
woefully inadequate. We could double, triple, or quadruple the funding.
It is important to recognize that we are discussing today the most important natural resource in our country. The Minister of State for Youth laughs when I say that the most important natural resource in this country is our young people. He may think the most important resource is coal, copper, platinum or uranium, but we believe that the most important natural resource is the people of Canada, and particularly the young people. We should invest in the development of that natural resource as we do in no other resource sector.
I know that when the Minister of State for Youth stands up he will say that there is no money to help young people, that all the programs to help young people had to be eliminated. I must remind the Minister that the Government thought it was appropriate to spend $9.5 billion to help the multinational oil companies. The Government thought it was appropriate to spend $1 billion to bail out two banks, which has never before been done on the face of the earth. The Government found it appropriate to spend billions of dollars to provide incentives for corporations to develop in central Canada. However, the Government cannot find the money to provide training, education, and job opportunities for our young people. That is the disgrace of it all.
The most dastardly blow of all was when we all received Hot-100, a quick guide to see what the feds are doing for youth. I challenge anyone to find something in this booklet which is available to really help young people. I have gone through it page by page as have my two sons. When I brought it home they got quite excited because they were not aware that the federal Government was doing anything to help young people and wanted to find out what it was doing. Those two young men went through this book page by page and when they finished they were disappointed. They made phone calls and found that a lot of these so-called programs had no money in them at all.
As an example, it talks about pension programs and a lot of university post-graduate degree programs which help some people. However, for 99.9 per cent of the young people needing assistance there is very little, if anything. I will not say there is absolutely nothing in here because there may be something which I have not found, but I look forward to hearing the Minister of State for Youth outline the programs in here which are in use today.
I looked through the report of Parliament which was an examination of the problems and issues facing Canadian youth between the ages of 15 and 24. There are pages and pages of recommendations, but I could not find any which have been implemented. Of all the recommendations that talk about ways to get young people back to work, none have been implemented. I wonder why Parliament bothered to do this if the Government is simply going to ignore the recommendations.

May 7, 1987
Supply
In talking to young people across the country I have sensed their despondency. Records show that alcoholism, drug abuse, suicides and attempted suicides, and drop-out rates in schools and training programs are worsening. I say that with great reluctance but the facts demonstrate that conclusively. It is now only fair to ask what the solutions are.
My hon. friend from Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador laid out a number of solutions as he saw them. They were good, thoughtful solutions and the Government should take action immediately. I want to propose some other solutions. They flow out of a very extensive task force which the NDP launched in 1985, chaired by the Hon. Member for Windsor- Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy). It travelled across the country from coast to coast. It visited major and minor communities, rural areas, high schools, technical schools, vocational schools and universities. The task force listened to 600 participants and received over 300 briefs. It resulted in a report which laid out all of the recommendations by the NDP in order to assist young people. I want to highlight some of them.
At the top of the list was a program called Youth Prospects which would provide a wide range of opportunities for young people. We felt it was appropriate to set aside ample funding so that young people could receive adequate support in developing their various skills. At a cost of about $6,000 a year they could choose from one of four options. They could undertake two years of job training, which would involve on-the-job training, classroom instruction, or a combination thereof. It would provide them with the necessary skills, expertise and experience to participate directly in the workforce after two years.
We also suggested a two-year entrepreneurialship program. We would provide seed money for young people to go out and develop a new business of one kind or another. This would help develop entrepreneurial skills, expertise and experience to assist them in creating jobs not only for themselves but for other young people as well.
We suggested a two-year program of life skills training. We recognize that a lot of our young people today lack some of the basic skills required to enter the workforce or continue with their education. This would help develop their literacy skills. It would help them to apply for jobs, fill out resumes and a whole host of other valuable life skills which, for a variety of reasons, some young people have not obtained over the years.
A fourth option was to provide, again, around $6,000 a year to assist young people to complete two years of post-secondary education. That could be vocational school, technical school, business school or secretarial school. It could mean one would go on to a college or university. Two years to develop those basic abilities and a sense of confidence which would encourage young people to go on with their training and education.
We suggested that program because at the moment the Government's support for students is in the form of loans more
often than not. If you want to complete your post-secondary education you can borrow $6,000, $7,000, or $8,000 year after year. That may be appropriate for a handful of young people, but for those in my constituency, where the unemployment rate is unfortunately in the 20 per cent range, it is simply impossible. They cannot even think about going on to technical school or university where the bill for the year might be $8,000 because they probably will not have even a summer job. We all know that only one out of three students is likely to obtain a summer job and the lion's share will be very low paid.

Those jobs will also tend to be restricted to central Canada where the economic forecasts are more healthy than in other parts of the country. I think we are all too well aware that of all the jobs created in this country last year, 96 per cent were in central Canada. If you are a young person seeking a summer job in Labrador, British Columbia, or central Alberta, you are going to have a difficult time because economic conditions in those parts of Canada are extremely difficult relative to central Canada.
We asked ourselves, why not provide a youth prospect fund and put dollars in the hands of young people so that if they take two years of job training, two years of entrepreneurial training, two years of life skills training, two years of postsecondary education, they will become a better person, a better citizen, and make Canada a better place? We would be investing this money in the future of our young people and therefore in the future of Canada.
In adding up the cost it would come to an additional $550 million in the first year. Compare that with the billions upon billions of dollars we give large corporations to do all kinds of things with. Compare it with the $1 billion we paid to bail out two banks. Compare it to the other things the Government spends money on. The money would put tens of thousands of young people back into school or in the workplace.
We say that is good. What are all those people going to do when they get their pay cheques? They will spend the money. It will be spent in their communities right across the country. It will help create more jobs. The various Governments will collect sales taxes as this money moves through the system. We calculate that the federal and provincial Governments would get the lion's share of that money back through improved economic conditions and the tax system. We are not talking about spending money, we are talking about investing in the most important natural resource Canada has, its young people.
I suspect that the Minister of State for Youth would really like to help young people. He would like to be doing a lot of things and perhaps implementing the suggestions offered by my friend and myself, steps that could be taken immediately to assist young people. I suspect that he personally would like to do that. However, he has to have the money. When he has no money in his Ministry, when his cabinet colleagues, particularly the Minister of Finance, refuse to give him the necessary
May 7, 1987

funds to develop those policies I am sure he would like to develop, it must be very frustrating for him.
In closing I want to say that I do not directly criticize the Minister of State for Youth although I must ask: Where is the money to help young people? I levy my criticism primarily at his cabinet colleagues who, for whatever reason, have decided not to provide the financial support to enable the Minister to invest in Canada's most important natural resource, its young people.

Member that we are not talking about just a federal program. We are talking about a national program, a national initiative to attempt to resolve the concerns and difficulties facing young people. As a Member of Parliament from British Columbia I have a great deal of concern when it comes to post-secondary education. When I look at the operating capital for our college and university system, including technical and vocational schools, I notice that when we look at the final budget, the total allocation of funds in the Province of British Columbia for post-secondary education, we see that its source is Ottawa. In other words, the federal Government is funding post-secondary education in the Province of British Columbia by 100 per cent. As a matter of fact, it is funding the province to the tune of 104 per cent. In other words, all of the money that Ottawa sends British Columbia for post-secondary education goes into postsecondary education and some of it is siphoned off for other uses. Yet the Province of British Columbia does not match one penny of the federal government contribution.
If the Province of British Columbia was doing what Parliament expected of it and what it had promised to do at one time, post-secondary educational opportunities in that province would be significantly enhanced. However, the province is not participating at all, and that is a provincial Government disgrace.

I think it is noteworthy that my two friends speak very strongly about this issue. The Hon. Member from the New Democratic Party says that this is one of the most critical issues facing the country, and he went on to say that youth are the most important natural resource in Canada.

I had planned to thank my official critics for their opening remarks, but I regret I cannot do that because it is not the case.
The tone of the speech by the Member from the NDP is particularly appropriate today. I want to share with him my own experience. When I was named to this portfolio in June, 1986, one of the first things I learned was that the debate about youth in this country was very partisan. I and all Members of the House will agree that the issue is political, but in the aftermath of the hunger strike by our colleague in the other place, the debate was very partisan.
Upon closer examination of the issue, and being a young politician myself, I discovered that if we want to be honest with Canadians, especially those young Canadians who suffer from a certain cynicism, according to the experience of the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap, I guess we must admit that all political parties at all levels have often used the issue of youth as a political vehicle.

I tell them, with a smile, that they will often hear politicians say that youth are the future of Canada, as though there were a choice between youth and something else. I do not know to what politicians are referring when they say youth are the

future of Canada because, of course, that is what they are. What else could happen?

I tell Canadians that the ultimate winner is when a politician says: "Youth are the most important natural resource of Canada". I say that to Canadians laughingly because 1 find it paternalistic and condescending. While I do not think politicians say that in bad faith, that single partisan characteristic of the debate is a major obstacle in identifying problems, developing a consensus, and designing solutions. It is an obstacle to recognizing the fact that the world has changed.
Let me move on to describe what we have done. One of my first objectives upon assuming this portfolio was to determine what was the most important problem facing young Canadian men and women. That is why I put that question to the two opposition Parties. However, I did not hear a clear answer. While the Government has found an answer, those Parties have much work to do.
In our effort to identify the most important problem facing youth, we examined the major studies and reports that have been published in this country over a number of years. I am referring to the Macdonald Commission Report, the Forget Report on Unemployment Insurance, the International Year of Youth Report, the Senate Youth Report, the report from the Province of Newfoundland, and more recently, the report of Ken Dryden, Youth Commissioner for the Province of Ontario. All of those reports, taken together, essentially converge to the same conclusion. It is that the most important problem facing young Canadian men and women today is the transition from school to work, particularly for young people who do not finish high school. That is the Government's conclusion, for the information of those Members opposite.
Having come to that conclusion, we proceeded to determine where Canada was headed. That is a very important consideration because the policy that is developed for young Canadians will not operate in a vacuum. It will have to work within a Canadian context as well as the larger world context.
According to 1984 statistics, Canada is second only to West Germany in our dependence on trade in terms of GNP. Therefore, if we choose to follow that course, as we have in our trade negotiations with the Americans and our negotiations at GATT, the natural consequence is that Canada will have to acquire, develop, and manage new technologies to support its position in the labour markets.
In order to pursue our course as a trading nation, and develop the new technologies to support that position, the last link in the chain is the development of labour market policies and human resources to acquire and develop the new technologies to support our position in the export markets.
Consequently, we went on to determine how the labour market in Canada is presently operating and found that there is a direct relationship between academic training and job security. More than half of those who were unemployed for six

May 7, 1987
Supply
months or more had not completed high school. The unemployment rate of those who fail to complete high school is three times that of youth with post-secondary training. In the last year of the recession in 1984, 75 per cent of those who were unemployed did not graduate from high school.
In light of these statistics, we moved on to examine how the labour market has changed through the years. Let me explain how the labour market has evolved from the 1950s to 1987.
In the fifties a young person in Canada could attend high school, drop out before graduation, and find a good job in a resource-based economy or, in a manufacturing economy like that of southern Ontario, find a good job in the automotive industry. If we want to draw a comparison between how the world has changed from the fifties to the eighties, the difference is that there are fewer and fewer jobs in Canada for unskilled labourers. Inasmuch as we can predict the future, there will be fewer and fewer jobs for unskilled labourers notwithstanding the fact that the growth in jobs in Canada is in the service sector.
We then came to what was for me and for the Government the most troubling problem we witnessed in that context. In Canada there is a link between training, holding a job, and the changing labour market. Notwithstanding that, 30 per cent to 40 per cent of young Canadian men and women-and it is something which neither Party opposite raised today-drop out of high school before graduation. That is dramatic. It is a great loss to the country now and it will be an even more important loss to the country in years to come.
Over and above that, it means much personal hardship for some young people who just fail to realize that by dropping out of high school they may be dropping out, to a certain extent, of active participation in the Canadian labour market in years to come.
In that context we then looked at how other countries dealt with the transition from school to work. For example, we looked at the United Kingdom, France, Sweden, Finland, and West Germany, and we found that in many cases the mechanisms in those countries for the transition were more developed and more sophisticated. The apprenticeship programs in West Germany, for example, were much more generic. The student or person entering the program had a specific status which he kept with him throughout the system. The same does not apply in Canada.
We are sensitive to the fact that we cannot just take a system from another country and implement it here. There are historical, sociological, and cultural factors which must be taken into account. However, we can borrow on some of the examples all over the world.
There were systems which were closer to ours. For example, co-op programs are familiar to Canadians. It is something with which they are comfortable and for which I found unanimous approval. It is part of the mechanisms into which we can look.
Having done all that, perhaps my colleagues will understand why we would find, according to the constitutional balance in Canada, which does not necessarily apply in other countries, that education is first and foremost a provincial jurisdiction. It is that to a certain extent, and I say that with reservations. I do not want to speak as a lawyer, but I should like to give an opinion. In terms of educating young people from the entry level to the secondary level, it may be unequivocal provincial jurisdiction. Once they reach the post-secondary level, and we are dealing with adults in training, obviously the federal Government plays an important role.
The obvious conclusion is that if we want to develop a national youth policy in that context, having identified a specific problem and the emerging consensus, we would go to the provinces. Being respectful, and in the spirit of national reconciliation about which we spoke, we would first go to the provinces to ask them whether they agreed that it was the most important problem.
Part of the paternalism and the partisanship surrounding the issue is that although everyone says it is our most important problem and that the youth is our future, no one, until we decided to do it, went to the extent of identifying it and asking other Canadians to join in the consensus. If they agree that it is the most important problem, the natural consequences flow from it.
I should like to report to the House at this point in time that I have visited eight Canadian provinces in less than a month. To give an indication of how much I travelled, the airlines have lost my luggage at least four times. We are doing this as rapidly as possible. Half of everything which goes into the Canadian Jobs Strategy goes to young people between the ages of 15 years and 24 years, approximately. It is a ballpark figure, but on average that is what it will be. In fiscal 1986-87 it will have been approximately $720 million. The issue is not whether it will be a new program. The Hot-100 illustrates that plentifully; there are over 100 programs which apply to young people.
The issue is that we must change the system; that is the real issue.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-YOUTH-EDUCATION AND EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: It is about time.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-YOUTH-EDUCATION AND EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Yes, it is about time. It is about time we sat down, if we are sincere and want to go beyond the partisanship of the debate, which is a real impediment to the finding of solutions in society.
Let me reiterate the fact that we have a sincere and real commitment to the issue. It is not enough to say that youth are the future of the country or that they are our most important natural resource.
There could be new programs for specific problems, but a new program with $10 million or $20 million will not change the fundamental problem. What is needed is a change in the system, and it will not happen overnight. However, it is to
May 7, 1987

what the Government is truly and sincerely committed under the leadership of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-YOUTH-EDUCATION AND EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-YOUTH-EDUCATION AND EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the analysis of the Minister, but I am not entirely clear on the impediment of partisan debate.
It seems to me that in what I said and what the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) said we very clearly analysed the problems. As a matter of fact, I think the Minister said that in his reply.
However, I am clear on the problem which he identified. He made the link-and I would like him to make it clearer- between lost luggage and the lost generation. What he said to us is that we must change the system and that he has been going about doing that by consulting.
However, where do we go from here? What we are looking for today, and what Canadian youth will be looking for, are some specific answers to how we address their very specific problems.
The Minister asked those of us in the Opposition to provide specific answers. I think we gave them. One was to make a change in the Canada Student Loans Program. That was very specific. It could be done starting today.
I know that there are wider problems. None of us underestimate the difficulties in coming to grips with them. We all know what the Constitution says. We all know what are the impediments.
I want the Minister to go beyond what he said and to tell us the outcome of losing luggage and visiting so many people in so many days in a struggle to come to grips with the problems of this lost generation. What is the linkage between lost luggage and the lost generation? What was the outcome of his travels? What will be some of the approaches? How do we bring in the provinces? How do we bring the various players to a national consensus?
What we have now, compared with the situation when we were the Government of Canada, is a national Government of one stripe and most provincial Governments of the same stripe. In essence it should perhaps be easier now than it was before, at least one would think, to come to grips with the jurisdictional problem. However, 1 did not hear today even the broad outlines of what will be the approach-bearing in mind and granting what the Minister said-to coming to grips with the problems in the system.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-YOUTH-EDUCATION AND EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not sure I understand the Hon. Member's question about the link between lost luggage and a lost generation. On the lost luggage side, I made that remark because I have been travelling a lot recently in this consultation process with the provinces. Airlines have had the opportunity, though not always through any fault of their own
Supply
but because of tight schedules, to send my luggage to places other than the ones to which I have been going.
On the lost generation side, I hope my hon. colleague is not among those who say that there is a lost generation. I find that a very unusual thing to say. That people would say there is a lost generation is an indication of failure. Man has been on earth for millions of years, and suddenly we are being asked to determine if one generation is better off than the previous one, a very unusual exercise.
Generations inherit problems from previous generations and civilization has the duty to do better than the preceding generation. Another unusual thing about the notion of a lost generation is that the premise of the assertion is that the previous generation found something. I do not know what it found, but I would be curious to find out.
We must recognize that the world has changed. Those who are consumed by the lost generation debate do not realize that the world and its problems have changed and are new. We have to face up to them.
The Hon. Member asked what we are doing to face up to those new problems. Perhaps he may have found by accident part of the answer for which he was looking. I told the Hon. Member what the most important problem is today and will be for the rest of the mandate, and I do not think I will find any disagreement with that.
Having identified the problem, we are trying to develop a consensus, to get the provinces to join with us in saying that this is the most important problem, and then looking at mechanisms to elaborate on training and education options that will be more viable for the 30 per cent or 40 per cent of young people who drop out. We should encourage young people to stay within the system because their training capability and transferable skills will be of paramount importance to their participation in labour markets in the years to come. The federal Government which already plays a very important role in apprenticeship training programs is willing to play an important and a leadership role in developing systems that will make the education and training systems of Canada more pertinent in the minds of the 30 per cent to 40 per cent of young people who drop out.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-YOUTH-EDUCATION AND EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister makes it particularly difficult to ask hard questions. He is a very decent fellow and he makes a very thoughtful presentation about the problems faced by many young people.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

The question I want to put to the Minister is not intended to be a tough one. We all recognize that long-term solutions have to be sought and implemented and that that will take time. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-YOUTH-EDUCATION AND EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me tell the Hon. Member of a series of things. If we want to understand the important changes that have taken place in the Ministry for Youth in recent months, we have to go back to 1986 when the Ministry was transferred from the Secretary of State to the Department of Employment and Immigration, acknowledging thus the fact that employment is one of the most important problems facing young Canadians today. This put at the disposal of the Ministry for Youth one of the most important federal government departments with 27,000 people and a great deal of resources. That occurred in the spring of 1986.
Second, there was a designation of a full 25 per cent of the Innovations budget under the Canadian Jobs Strategy for youth-related projects, and we have exceeded that minimum target. The youth council that was requested was granted by the federal Government. The Hon. Member referred to his own Party's task force report on entrepreneurship. A $10 million initiative was provided for that in co-operation with the federal Government, the private sector and the non-profit sector in the form of YMCAs. There are nine centres across Canada, eight of which are exclusively for young people, helping people develop entrepreneurial skills.
Over three years, $10 million will be provided to this very innovative program under which the federal Government allots money on a set price per job basis in each region. Thirty per cent is allotted on the signing up of a young person, another 30 per cent is allotted when the course is terminated, and another 40 per cent is allotted a year after the young person has been in business. That is a very original funding formula of which we are very proud because it is result-driven. This was something that was suggested by a non-profit organization.
Another $2.9 million went to Youth Employment Skills to open four centres in Canada. We announced $180 million for Challenge '87. I know there has been some debate in the
House about that because it was $30 million for youth last summer because of the census but there is no census this year.
Approximately 70 per cent of those who benefit from summer student programs under Challenge '87 are postsecondary students. We are happy about that because we know they need the money to go back to school. However, those who suffer the most are those who have dropped out. For that reason, within the Challenge '87 structure, we doubled the budget of the work-orientation workshops component from $4 million to $8 million. That is something of which the Government is very proud. Work-orientation workshops identify potential drop-outs within the school system at the secondary level and offer them training during the summer. We found that 70 per cent of them go back into the school system and that those who choose not to go back at least do so in full knowledge of the consequence of their choice. That is something in which the Government takes a lot of pride.
I know that the Hon. Member's 17-year-old son did not find anything in the Hot-100. He mentioned in particular the reference to the Canada Pension Plan. I am surprised that Hon. Members would feel that we are wasting time by informing young people about the Canada Pension Plan. I believe about 100,000 young people benefit from the Canada Pension Plan. By looking through this book, a young person at le Salon International de la Jeunesse found information on the Canada Pension Plan and is now receiving benefits.
Perhaps this book is of no use to the Hon. Member's son, but it has been of some use to young Canadian men and women and those who work with them who want to know what programs are available for young people. What does the federal Government have to offer, to where does one write, and to whom does one talk? Those are the questions this booklet attempts to answer, and that is its only pretence.
We have announced a national forum on post-secondary education to be held in Saskatoon, which should answer a great deal of the-

subsubtopic: IMPORTANCE OF SMALL BUSINESS IN JOB CREATION-ALLEGED FORGETFULNESS OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Yesterday, in his statement to the House concerning the tax reform, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) failed completely to address the issue of small businesses, in spite of the fact that Hon. Members have repeatedly emphasized in the House that small businesses are responsible for over 70 per cent of all jobs created in Canada. Yet, in such an important speech, not once did he refer to them. Not a word, Mr. Speaker.
While carrying out its proposed reform of the corporate income tax system, will the Government make sure that small businesses continue to benefit from the present reduced income tax rate structure?
In its reform of the federal sales tax system, is it planning to exempt small businesses from value added taxes, national multi-stage sales taxes and business transfer taxes?
How could an industry which creates so many jobs in Canada ... If the Government helped each and every small business to create one job, we would end up with 750,000 more new jobs in Canada. The Minister of Finance just does not understand that this industry plays a vital and significant role in the Canadian economy, and he does not even mention it in making such an important speech. That is unbelievable!

subtopic: IMPORTANCE OF FOREST RESOURCES TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES
IMPORTANCE OF FOREST RESOURCES TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, from the time of the first settlement of this country until today forests have played a key role in the survival and growth of the Atlantic provinces. Forests occupy some two-thirds of our total land area. They provide over 50,000 direct and indirect jobs and account for $1.7 billion in exports throughout the region.
[ Translation]
Several of our communities depend entirely on our forest resources for their survival.
Our Government recognized the important role our forest industry plays in this area. Through its Canadian Forestry Service, it contributes $135 million, thereby assuming 60 per cent of the whole forest renewal and improvement costs under federal and provincial agreements. A significant amount is spent improving private woodlots, including those producing Christmas and maple trees.

We are committed to working with provincial Governments, industry, and small private landowners to improve our knowledge of forest dynamics and management through ongoing programs of research.

subtopic: CANCELLATION OF AIRLINE LICENCE-SUGGESTED APPOINTMENT OF ARBITRATOR
CANCELLATION OF AIRLINE LICENCE-SUGGESTED APPOINTMENT OF ARBITRATOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Fred Turner case exemplifies the best and worst in human behaviour. Mr. Turner displays the patience of Job in his two-month vigil here on Parliament Hill. The understanding and charity he shows towards his adversaries who put him out of business disguise an inner strength and sense of purpose which has kept him going from office to office in search of justice. He seeks only to have an independent arbitrator assigned to evaluate his claim and mediate with the Government-simple natural justice and nothing more.
For over a year my colleagues and I have worked on this issue and allowed Mr. Turner to call upon our resources to put his case forward because we believe it is just. I also wish to commend members of the other two Parties who have taken up his cause, including those who were part of the Government at the time this wrong occurred. They have the courage to admit some responsibility.
Specific mention is due to the former Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport, the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour), who had the intestinal fortitude to stand up for Mr. Turner and has offered the resources of his office as well. This is the best in human behaviour. The worst can be seen in the Government that took his business and is now allowing Mr. Turner and his family to suffer.
The Government has released misinformation about the Turner case in the hope of diffusing his arguments and has refused independent examination of the facts so that the true extent of the wrongs will never be known. Cabinet Members have disgraced themselves in the eyes of fair-minded Canadians. Shame on them.

May 7, 1987

subtopic: PROPOSED WHITE PAPER-SUPPORT FOR EXPECTED CONTENTS
PROPOSED WHITE PAPER-SUPPORT FOR EXPECTED CONTENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many Canadians welcomed the announcement made yesterday by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) that a White Paper on a comprehensive tax reform package will be tabled in the House on June 18 of this year. The theme will be greater fairness and equity for individual Canadians.
Most Canadians will have more take-home pay after the changes. The personal income tax rates will decrease, there will be three brackets rather than 10, and less total tax dollars will come from individuals. The tax credit option will be more widely used since it is a fairer method. A tax deduction, on the other hand, is of more value the higher the income. Tax credits will be of direct help to senior citizens and lower-income families.
While corporate tax rates are expected to decrease, there will be a significant increase in the tax dollars from the business sector by shutting down certain preferences. Some business groups are not paying their fair share of taxes. A business transfer tax is also likely, we are told, and I urge the Minister to permit very few exceptions in order to minimize the paperwork and the complexity of the system.
Finally, I hope the provincial sales tax systems can be harmonized with the federal system to increase simplicity and fairness.

subtopic: NEED FOR GOVERNMENT TO RECOGNIZE WORK OF ALL MOTHERS AND TO HELP THEM
NEED FOR GOVERNMENT TO RECOGNIZE WORK OF ALL MOTHERS AND TO HELP THEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to remind Hon. Members that across Canada next Sunday, May 10, will be Mothers' Day, a special day dedicated to all mothers, whether they are 20 or 80.
I would like to take this opportunity to ask the Government to move rapidly in helping many Canadian families, recognizing the work of all mothers, whether they work in or outside the home. It would be important that the Government help women who do full-time work at home, by offering them credits or access to a pension fund.
Many other mothers work outside the home, often because of economic necessity. For the latter, it would be important that the Government have quality care services, together with parent holidays and access to part-time, well-paid jobs.
This certainly would help many families worry less, both financially and in terms of their children's welfare.
I want to wish every mother a bright Mothers' Day, on which everyone recognizes their importance in Canadian society.

subtopic: SUPPORT FOR LEGISLATION TO CURB ABUSES
SUPPORT FOR LEGISLATION TO CURB ABUSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) for tabling legislation this week which tackles the problem of pornography head on. For too long women and children have been exploited through violence and degrading pornography. This piece of legislation sends a clear message to those who profit through the exploitation of others. At the same time it continues to respect our freedom of expression.
I reject the comments of those who disagree with this Bill. I suggest that they produce a better definition of pornography. We would be glad to consider all suggestions that might improve the Bill.
Pornography touches all of us and I call upon all those who would like to see this blight removed to speak up now and support the Minister of Justice.

subtopic: USE OF ALBERTA TELEPHONE LINES TO TRANSMIT ALLEGED RACIST MESSAGE
USE OF ALBERTA TELEPHONE LINES TO TRANSMIT ALLEGED RACIST MESSAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, racism is being offered to the people of Alberta on telephone lines owned by the province. Every Sunday night the so-called Church of Jesus Christ Christian-Aryan Nations offers a new message to tempt listeners into racist views of the world.
The authorities have allowed this abomination to continue without interruption. The Alberta Government has refused to act and wants to maintain silence on the matter. Complaints by the League for Human Rights of B'nai Brith to the Canadian Human Rights Commission and the Commissioner himself have produced no apparent action.
Is the Government of Canada ignorant of this abuse of our telecommunications system? Has the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) considered action and decided to do nothing? Does the Conservative Party of Canada as well as the Conservative Party of Alberta condone the racism of the Aryan Nations in western Canada? Surely the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) would expect speedy action if he were informed of these activities.
May 7, 1987

subtopic: CRITICISM OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY'S TAX PROBE REPORT
CRITICISM OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY'S TAX PROBE REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, cashing in on the general dissatisfaction with an overly complex and burdensome tax system would seem to be a sure way for opposition Parties to score points. This was evidently the idea behind the NDP tax probe exercise, but it has obviously backfired on them.
