subtopic: VICTIMS OF VIOLENT CRIMES-CALL FOR EXPANSION OF RESTITUTION PROVISIONS
VICTIMS OF VIOLENT CRIMES-CALL FOR EXPANSION OF RESTITUTION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada's criminal justice system is ignoring the rights of victims of violent crimes. While perpetrators of brutal attacks are freed after serving brief or part of brief sentences, their victims, who are often left physically and mentally scarred for life, are all but forgotten.
I urge the Minister to act quickly in drafting the appropriate legislation which would amend the Criminal Code by expanding the now meagre restitution provisions therein. I also ask the Minister to consider in his amendment the use of victim impact statements in the sentencing of violent criminals. An amendment of this nature could only serve to ensure that penalties for violent crimes are appropriate for the crimes committed and as precedence for due restitution for victims of violent crimes.
In addition, the Government should take steps to increase the power of the justice system in meeting the immediate needs and concerns of crime victims by increasing and enriching available government services for all victims of crime.

Mr. Speaker, after the statement made yesterday by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on the matter of tax reform, I would urge Canadian families and senior citizens to look out and be prepared to fight. Hon. Members will remember that this Government-and I would like to recall the consultation it made in January 1985 with the Blue Paper, when senior citizens and families were misled by the same Minister of Finance who promised to fully reindex Old Age Security pensions, after he had cut them-promised at that point that family allowance cuts would not be used to reduce the deficit, misleading Canadian families once more.
I am warning the Minister of Finance there will be an allout war if this Government changed senior citizens' tax exemptions, if that is not completely transferred in respect of senior citizens. And also if the exemption for dependent children, if it is transferred for families with children, there will be an all-out war and the Minister will have to recognize his error once again, as he did on the matter of deindexing Old Age Security pensions.

maintopic: GREATER USE OF GRAIN URGED FOR PRODUCTION OF ETHANOL
GREATER USE OF GRAIN URGED FOR PRODUCTION OF ETHANOL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a year and five days ago the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources put forward its report, which was unanimous, to this House. It concerned a market for surplus Canadian grains which would provide an unparalleled economic opportunity for our farmers and reduce dependence on imports and fossil fuels.
This week the Western Canadian Wheat Growers Association is again urging federal and provincial Governments to take a serious look at ethanol production as a means of providing an alternative domestic market for western grains, diversifying the western economy, and developing value-added industries for western agricultural products.
The use of ethanol, an alcohol which can be produced from grain, as a replacement for lead in gasoline, could provide a domestic market for over eight million tonnes of Canadian cereal grain if 10 per cent ethanol were used to provide the octane requirements of Canadian gasoline. A three per cent ethanol and five per cent methanol blend, as currently used in Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba, would consume almost six per cent of Canada's total cereal production.

May 7, 1987
Oral Questions
A window of opportunity is opening up. Allowable lead levels in Canada disgracefully still stand at 10 times the level allowed in the United States.
The Western Canadian Wheat Growers Association has recommended that the federal Government implement a program to provide the economic climate needed to kick-start the Canadian ethanol industry and provide a better environment for Canadians, including an accelerating lead phase-down program which would effectively eliminate lead in gasolines by 1990, and an environmental ban on the heavy metal octane enhancer, MMT, which has been banned in the United States since 1978.
The operations of the Western Accord and the supposed free market in refined petroleum products are being used to suppress a domestic Canadian industry which could serve the objectives of fairness for the farm economy rather than the objectives of the multinational oil industry.
The Government should not fund the MBTE plants. Instead, we must diversify, distribute jobs, and provide a market for Canadian farm production.

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO FUND RAISERS FOR WOODSTOCK PROJECT TO AID MENTALLY RETARDED
TRIBUTE TO FUND RAISERS FOR WOODSTOCK PROJECT TO AID MENTALLY RETARDED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Governments should take note that voluntary community efforts can still raise funds for good causes without the help of tax dollars. Last Sunday afternoon I had the pleasure of opening the new headquarters building for the Woodstock and District Association for the Mentally Retarded. This new building, known as ARC Industries, provides employment facilities for 84 mentally-handicapped people and has a staff of 45. It complements a residence and school which were built some years ago.
The recent project began two years ago. Since then plans have been developed, and funds in the amount of over $750,000 were raised within the community. The single largest donation of $100,000 came from the Rotary Club of Woodstock. The balance was raised with smaller donations from groups and individuals in the area. At the time of the official opening there was only a minuscule $13,000 still owing on the project.
This amazing achievement is testimony to the fact that volunteerism is still alive and that, given a good project and imaginative and dedicated leadership, Canadians will respond to the needs of a community without financial help from Governments.

subtopic: IMPORTANCE OF TOURISM INDUSTRY TO ECONOMY
IMPORTANCE OF TOURISM INDUSTRY TO ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, "Canada grows with tourism" is the theme of this year's National Tourism Week which will take place May 11 to May 17. I believe the theme is entirely appropriate considering that tourism generates over $22 billion in domestic revenues and provides over 600,000 direct jobs to Canadians. If properly nurtured it could employ over one million Canadians by the year 2000.

Mr. Speaker, tourism is one of Canada's major assets. Not only does the industry create hundreds of thousands of jobs, but tourism helps promote harmony and goodwill among the various regions of Canada. It is an asset for national unity.
Tourism also plays a leading role in promoting world peace, an objective which all Canadians have at heart.
I would be remiss if I failed to congratulate the Tourism Industry Association of Canada for supporting National Tourism Week, and I urge all Canadian men and women to participate actively in National Tourism Week.

subsubtopic: FORTHCOMING WHITE PAPER-PREVIOUS GOVERNMENT MEASURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. After two and a half years middle and low-income Canadians know that they have been the target of more than $22 billion worth of Conservative Government tax grabs. They are paying more sales tax, more excise tax and more income tax.
Yesterday the Minister announced that he would table his tax reform proposals in a White Paper in June. Can the Minister assure the House today that his reform will undo all, not just some, of his own huge tax grabs?

subsubtopic: FORTHCOMING WHITE PAPER-PREVIOUS GOVERNMENT MEASURES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FORTHCOMING WHITE PAPER-PREVIOUS GOVERNMENT MEASURES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, one of the reasons personal income taxes are up is because we have 750,000 more people working and paying taxes, which contributes to personal tax revenues.

subsubtopic: FORTHCOMING WHITE PAPER-PREVIOUS GOVERNMENT MEASURES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FORTHCOMING WHITE PAPER-PREVIOUS GOVERNMENT MEASURES
speechtext:
We have made a number of adjustments to the tax system. A number of those changes have resulted in greater fairness in the tax system. We have a
May 7, 1987

minimum tax. We have removed a number of the tax gimmicks that have been used, such as the Scientific Research Tax Credit, carve-outs, and the rules on limited partnerships, all of which have made personal income tax fair play. So, yes, we will address some further problems in tax reform. My friend will be very much aware of these on June 18.

subsubtopic: FORTHCOMING WHITE PAPER-PREVIOUS GOVERNMENT MEASURES
speechtext: Canadians are paying more taxes because the Minister increased the rates. I do not know how he can call a 33 per cent hike in sales tax fair.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Minister said that he may introduce a new consumption tax which he now calls a national multi-stage sales tax. The Minister knows that when New Zealand brought in its consumption tax the cost of living went up immediately by some 5 per cent. How much does the Minister expect the cost of living for Canadians to increase as a result of his new tax?
Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member is jumping ahead of herself. We will have a White Paper on June 18. This type of question will be addressed very clearly in the White Paper.

Mr. Speaker, last summer the Minister backed away from the idea of a value added tax in favour of a business transfer tax. We understand that in response to pressure from his cabinet colleagues, yesterday he backed away from the business transfer tax in favour of a national multi-stage sales tax, and said that some of the provinces were interested in it. Which provinces are interested in replacing provincial and federal sales taxes with a regressive new tax on every conceivable consumer item and service?

Mr. Speaker, again, I think the Hon. Member is jumping ahead of herself. We will be publishing a White Paper which will have a core proposal on a comprehensive multi-stage sales tax, as 1 indicated yesterday. At the last meeting of federal and provincial Ministers of Finance, a number of the provinces encouraged me to keep the option open of having either a federal and provincial tax of that nature, plus two federal only options of a business transfer tax or federal value added tax. These options are available to us, but they all centre around that core proposal of a comprehensive multi-stage tax.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. A couple of months ago, in response to a charge that he was the taxingest finance minister in Canadian history, he said:
What we have been doing here, John-
That is, John Ferguson of Southam News:
Oral Questions
-is to bring the level of taxation back to where it had been in the middle 70s.
Previous Ministers of Finance had let go of the tax reins and the level of
taxation as a per cent of income had gone down and down-
In bringing the level of taxation up and up, is it necessary to increase the worries of ordinary Canadians that perhaps even their food will be taxed? Will the Government tax even our daily bread? Canadians will never forgive the Government for that trespass.

Mr. Speaker, I have made it very clear that tax reform is not designed to increase the amount of revenues that the Government of Canada would take as a per cent of the national income of the country. That still stands.
It is obvious that the Minister is unwilling to say whether there will be a general tax on food.

Mr. Speaker, we know that beginning on July 1, the Minister will bring in a tax on snack food. He will put a new tax on popcorn, nuts, icecream bars, granola bars, pretzels, cheezies, potato chips, and even popsicles.
Oh, oh!

Does the Minister of Finance not realize that Canadian children only have so much money for an allowance, only so much for recess time, and can only take in so many empty pop bottles to get a bit of change in their pockets? Will he cancel this sneaky summer snack attack?
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, 1 can see that the Hon. Member will take off weight this summer.
I ask the Hon. Member to cast his attention back to my statement yesterday. I said that the result of tax reform will be that an overwhelming majority of Canadians will discover that they have more money in their pockets. They will be paying less tax. That is the objective of tax reform and the objective that I have set out very clearly. I think the Hon. Member will find that he will be very pleased with the results of tax reform come June 18.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. He has committed himself to let Canadians know on June 18 his plans for tax reform. However, he now seems to be trying to fudge that by saying he will put forth three or four options, the value added tax, the business transfer tax, and a new national sales tax imposed in co-operation with the provinces if they agree.

May 7, 1987
Oral Questions
Will the Minister assure the Elouse that the Government will state which of the sales tax options it favours when it issues its June 18 paper? Will he also assure the House that necessities like food will continue to be exempt?

Mr. Speaker, again the Hon. Member is pre-empting the whole process. We will have a White Paper. In the White Paper there will be a core proposal on how we will move to a comprehensive multistage sales tax.
There are three means by which we can operate that tax, three ways by which we can facilitate it, three mechanisms that we can use. I have said that those are open for consultation.
The provinces have indicated that they are interested in discussing one. We will be consulting with the private sector on the other two, as well as on the national sales tax.
There are options open to us on how we proceed, and that is what will flow from the White Paper in June.
[ Translation]

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER FOOD PRODUCTS WILL BE TAXED
INQUIRY WHETHER FOOD PRODUCTS WILL BE TAXED
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. After four of five answers the Minister has yet to indicate clearly whether food products will be taxed, even though a tax on food will cost the average Canadian family $300 in additional taxes on a basic life necessity. Can the Minister assure us and the House that such a basic necessity as food will not be taxable? Does the Minister quite simply intend to reduce income taxes while at the same time extending the sales tax to something as basic as food and daily bread?

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER FOOD PRODUCTS WILL BE TAXED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have told the Hon. Member and the other questioner that we are not going to pre-empt the process.
There are options, which I have set out, on the mechanisms we are going to use to implement that tax, some of which have the flexibility for exemptions. I think we must let the process run its course.
When the Hon. Member talks about the regressive nature of sales tax, I ask him to consider whether the current approach to sales tax without a refundable sales tax credit is the right way, or whether one with a refundable sales credit, which helps those with lower incomes finance the cost of sale tax, is a more progressive way of doing things. I think that is something we will be exploring again during the process of consultation.

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER FOOD PRODUCTS WILL BE TAXED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always understood that a White Paper was a statement of policy and that if the Government wanted to put forward options, which it has had the chance to do over the last two and a half years, it could come
up with a Green Paper or possibly a Yellow Paper if it were scared of the reaction of Canadians to a tax on food.

Mr. Speaker, is the Minister now intending to implement the proposals for personal and corporate taxes for 1988? Is it his real intention to hide behind these options and save the bad news on sales tax until after the 1989 campaign?

Mr. Speaker, it is a White Paper. I have made it clear yesterday, and I have said it again three times. I will say it once again for the Hon. Member-there will be one proposal on a comprehensive multi-stage sales tax. There are three mechanisms which we can use to implement that proposal. That is what we will be discussing with the interested parties following the release of the paper.
As far as the time is concerned, I think the Hon. Member will have to wait. The whole process of timing, consultation, legislation, and implementation will be set out at the time of the White Paper.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT GIVE COMMITMENT TO RETAIN REDUCED TAX RATES FOR SMALL BUSINESSES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Yesterday he completely forgot about small business. In his remarks on the tax reform he did not say a word about it. Some 70 per cent of new jobs in Canada are created by small and medium-sized businesses, and if each such company is encouraged to create one more job, unemployment in this country will be drastically reduced. With respect to his tax system proposition as it applies to corporations, is the Minister committed to retain reduced tax rates for small businesses to encourage them to expand and create yet more jobs?

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT GIVE COMMITMENT TO RETAIN REDUCED TAX RATES FOR SMALL BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government has never forgotten small business, unlike the Party of which he is a Member. We have never forgotten small business. In every Budget I have introduced in the House there has been something which has helped small business create jobs.
Perhaps the Hon. Member would care to reflect on the
750,000	jobs that have been created, an outstanding job-creation record. One of the reasons for that is that the
May 7, 1987

Government has supported the small business community, and that support will continue.

Mr. Speaker, small businessmen are fed up with rhetoric from the Minister of Finance. They want action. Whether there will be a business transfer tax, a value added tax or a national multistage sales tax, small businesses will pay more. Will the Minister announce today that under the new tax reform, small businesses will be exempted from federal sales taxes so they can create new jobs? Stop kidding and tell people how it is.
Mr. Speaker, I would be happy to invite the Hon. Member to meetings I have had with members of the small business community-
I had them too.

He says he did. Once in a while he does. If he would care to join me, he will see that what I am saying is not rhetoric.
My colleague just reminded me that John Bulloch, the President of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, has referred either to my last Budget or the one before that as being a block-buster Budget, a Budget that would help the small business community create more jobs. That is what the Government stands for.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance knows only too well that since he has been Minister of Finance we have seen personal income tax rates increase. According to the comment he made yesterday, they will now decrease.
My question is very straightforward. Is the Minister of Finance prepared to say that after his tax reform package has been introduced, Canadians who pay personal taxes, federal taxes and excise taxes will actually be paying less federal tax, or will they be paying more?
Mr. Speaker, 1 am not quite sure I understand what the Hon. Member means when he says less federal tax. Could he explain that to me? He has made a very general statement.

Mr. Speaker, 1 hope that this is not a supplementary question but I suspect that it is. After the tax reform the Minister has in mind, if an average Canadian were to add up the federal tax, the personal tax, the federal excise tax and the federal sales tax he or she pays, will the amount of money he or she will be paying be more or less than today?
Oral Questions
Mr. Speaker, if I got everything the Hon. Member said, after tax reform the average Canadian-I think I will expand on what he said-a good majority of Canadians will be paying less tax.

subsubtopic: PRIME MINISTER'S TOUR OF PRAIRIE PROVINCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. Last night the Conservative Party filled only half the hall in Lethbridge, Alberta, and gave the Prime Minister a very cool reception. Since Tories are not willing to come out to meet the Prime Minister and are giving him a cool reception, will the Deputy Prime Minister change the tour so that ordinary farmers and representatives of farm organizations will have an opportunity to meet with the Prime Minister to tell him of their concerns? speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: PRIME MINISTER'S TOUR OF PRAIRIE PROVINCES

subsubtopic: PRIME MINISTER'S TOUR OF PRAIRIE PROVINCES

subtopic: REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER MEET FARMERS
REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER MEET FARMERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are told that the only farm meeting the Prime Minister is having during the entire four-day tour is with the President of the local PC Association and 15 hand-picked farmers in Saskatoon. Can the Deputy Prime Minister say why the President of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool and representatives of other farm organizations like the NFU were not invited to this meeting? On a tour of this length, why is the Prime Minister not meeting with general farm organizations and with farmers, thousands of whom are wondering what his policy will be?

subtopic: REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER MEET FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this Prime Minister has met more often and more frequently with farm leaders then any other Prime Minister in the history of Canada. Day after day, this Hon. Member rises to pose questions and I really do not know where he gets his information.
The Hon. Member should know that the Prime Minister will be meeting again with farm leaders either in the last week of

May 7, 1987
Oral Questions
May or in the first week of June before he leaves to take the message to the summit meeting on behalf of Canadian agriculture.
This time the Prime Minister wants to do something I like to do, and I am sure all Members in the House like to do and that is not only to meet with farm leaders on a regular and frequent basis but to have the opportunity once in a while to talk to farmers who cannot come to Ottawa on a regular basis. That is exactly what he is doing.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. As the Deputy Prime Minister knows, the Prime Minister took his travelling road show to Lethbridge last night and was met with less than enthusiasm by staunch Conservative supporters.
Why did the Prime Minister not make two announcements last night, announcements western farmers want to hear now? Why did he not announce that there would be a sufficient deficiency payment for the 1987-88 crop year and why did he not announce the reversal of the lifting of the moratorium on FCC loans? Why did he not do that rather than give western Canadians another Trudeau-style lecture about Canada?

Mr. Speaker, it is very obvious why the Prime Minister did not make those announcements when he was in western Canada. The Prime Minister is simply keeping the commitment my colleague, the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board, and I made when we met with farm leaders on March 5. A very strong warning was sent out at that time that indeed we do not need to send out messages that would encourage farmers to do certain things other than to plan their 1987 cropping patterns based on market signals. That was the message that was sent, and I have said that over and over again. If the Hon. Member does not have a copy of that press release, I would be happy to have the one in front of me copied and sent across to him for his information.

Mr. Speaker, since the Minister is obviously ignoring the wheat pools' recent call for a commitment on a deficiency payment now, perhaps the Deputy Prime Minister can tell the House why, when the Prime Minister made one of his very rare appearances in western Canada, he did not announce the Government's long-awaited western diversification plan? Why is the Government taking so long to announce its plans? Why is it so slow?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, very simply, if we had announced a plan without consulting with westerners, farmers, the energy sector and other groups as the Prime
Minister is now doing, the Hon. Member would have condemned our action. This Government consults. It works with the provinces and the industries.
With the wheat pools?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It works with the wheat pools, and I must take exception, as I am sure the wheat pools will, to the cheap political opportunism in which the Hon. Member is engaged. The members of the pools indicated that, if it was convenient, they would be prepared to meet with the Prime Minister but that they have met with him on various occasions and will be meeting with him again. I wish the Hon. Member would stop using the wheat pools as a cheap political trick. It does him no good and it does the wheat pools no good.

subsubtopic: FORD'S PURCHASE OF VERSATILE FARM IMPLEMENT COMPANY-PROTECTION OF WORKERS' JOBS
speechtext:

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FORD'S PURCHASE OF VERSATILE FARM IMPLEMENT COMPANY-PROTECTION OF WORKERS' JOBS

network? As the Minister knows, that network is extraordinarily important and valuable to the farmers of western Canada. Can we get the assurance that the Government will hold Ford to its commitment to maintain those dealerships?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I am not aware of the allegations that the Hon. Member has made. subsubtopic: POTENTIAL FOR CIVIL RIGHTS VIOLATIONS

subsubtopic: DENIAL OF COMPENSATION TO CERTAIN PRISONERS OF WAR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Veterans Affairs. It concerns those Canadians, mainly from Newfoundland, who were held in a concentration camp in Algeria during World War II. Those veterans are being denied benefits as prisoners of war due to a technicality, as the Minister knows. The Minister has a reputation for giving veterans the benefit of the doubt if there is any dispute between them and the Department.

subsubtopic: DENIAL OF COMPENSATION TO CERTAIN PRISONERS OF WAR
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: DENIAL OF COMPENSATION TO CERTAIN PRISONERS OF WAR
speechtext:
Given that reputation, and since there is absolutely no doubt at all that those Canadians were indeed prisoners of war, will the Minister assure the House and those
Oral Questions
veterans that they will have their claims approved by his Department?

speakeroldname: Hon. George Hees (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subsubtopic: DENIAL OF COMPENSATION TO CERTAIN PRISONERS OF WAR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to compliment the Hon. Member for Beaches for, as usual, putting his question very simply and accurately. However, I am very sympathetic to the idea of doing everything possible to deal with deserving cases. With that in mind my officials have been working on a solution to this problem which will be brought forward just as soon as possible.

subsubtopic: DENIAL OF COMPENSATION TO CERTAIN PRISONERS OF WAR
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, just before Question Period I spoke to Mr. Jim Templeton, one of those prisoners, and he tells me they have been waiting since 1976 for the amendments to be brought before the House. speakeroldname: Hon. George Hees (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is well aware of what the Department of Veterans Affairs has been able to do to speed up the pension process greatly. I agree with him that this matter has been hanging fire far too long. I must also tell him it is one of those matters that was not brought to my attention earlier. Now that it has been I can assure him that I abhor delay just as much as he does and this matter will be brought forward and dealt with just as soon as it is possible to do so. I cannot do it any quicker than that.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Minister of Veterans Affairs. He can take another bow or two and the House will not mind. We are pleased with the tone of his answers today. It is much better than yesterday's answers by the individual sitting in for him.
The 1976 Compensation for Former Prisoners of War Act says that compensation can be paid to those Canadian servicemen who were held by a power engaged in activities against the Allies. Would the Minister not agree that Vichy France, which held those 22 Canadians at Laghouat, Algeria, was a power engaged in activities against the allied forces? speakeroldname: Hon. George Hees (Minister of Veterans Affairs):

Mr. Speaker, the country concerned has always been considered by this Government as a neutral country during World War II. For that reason it is impossible, I am advised, to pay this compensation. However, as I said to the Hon. Member for

May 7, 1987

Beaches, now that the matter has come to my attention I am very sympathetic.

I ask him to move as expeditiously as possible.

speakeroldname: Hon. George Hees (Minister of Veterans Affairs):

All I can
say once again is that the particular Government concerned was always considered by the Canadian Government to be a power not engaged in warfare with the Canadian Government. That is that. subsubtopic: FIRST STEP IN DETERMINATION PROCEDURE-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Immigration and is with regard to the new refugee legislation which Rabbi Gunther Plaut, author of a government commissioned study on refugees, described as paramount to "building a Berlin Wall around Canada".
In answer to my question in the House yesterday the Minister said: "the first step is not a pre-screening. It is a first step to a claimant's right to demonstrate whether he has a personal fear of persecution".
May 7, 1987

Will the Minister now come clean and acknowledge that this answer was completely false, that a claimant from a safe third country has no right to present his claim, has no opportunity to prove and be judged on his personal fear of persecution, and will be refused entry to the refugee board and sent packing? subsubtopic: FIRST STEP IN DETERMINATION PROCEDURE-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think the Member has read the Bill. In fact, he may not have even bought the newspaper which had a graph which clearly illustrated the steps. I would be happy to send it to him.
It is clear that in the first step the claimant is met by the adjudicator and a member of the independent Refugee Determination Board. They have two tests, the first of which is objective criteria. Does he have refugee status established elsewhere? Is he returnable to a safe third country?
Notwithstanding that, they listen thoughtfully because there is another low threshold discretion which allows them, if they believe there is even a slim chance that the life, limb or liberty of that person is at risk, to refer him to step two within 10 days to begin a hearing before the independent Refugee Determination Board.

subsubtopic: FIRST STEP IN DETERMINATION PROCEDURE-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister should stop right now manipulating and misleading public opinion. He knows that he cannot have it both ways.

subsubtopic: FIRST STEP IN DETERMINATION PROCEDURE-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: EFFECT OF NEW LEGISLATION ON OTHER COUNTRIES

Mr. Speaker, my question of privilege, for which I gave you notice, relates to inaccurate or improper information which impairs the ability of the House to come to a judgment about matters put before it.
In answering a question in the House yesterday about the Government's proposed refugee determination system, at page 5796 of Hansard, the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) intentionally or unintentionally misled the House when he said: "the first step is not a pre-screening. It is a first step to a claimant's right to demonstrate whether he has a personal fear of persecution".
The Minister said that the claimant had the right to demonstrate whether he has a personal fear of persecution, that the first step is not a bar to his right.
I would ask you to note, Mr. Speaker, the use of the word "right", which in common parlance and in law means a power that a person possesses by law that he can assert. I would ask you, Sir, to note also the use of the words "personal fear", which indicate subjective criteria. It indicates that the claimant's personal feelings will prevail or be considered.
I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that anyone reading this reply would assume that the claimant in all instances can present his case and have it judged on the merits. This is just not so. It is clear from the legislation that many claimants will be barred from presenting their personal cases if they fall into a certain category of claimants, namely, if they came to Canada from a safe third country. This will be an absolute bar to their claim. No discretion will be given to the adjudicator and the refugee board member who presides at the initial hearing. There will be no opportunity to present a case, and the Minister, I would suggest, is wrong to say that the claimant has a right to demonstrate a personal fear-

Mr. Speaker, I based my answer on Clause 48.1 of the proposed Bill C-55. It states:
48.1 (1) A person who claims to be a Convention refugee is not eligible to have
the claim determined by the Refugee Division if
(a)	the claimant has been recognized by any country, other than Canada, as a Convention refugee and has been issued a valid and subsisting travel document by that country pursuant to Article 28 of the Convention;
(b)	the claimant came to Canada from a country that has been prescribed as a safe third country for all persons or for persons of a specified class of persons of which the claimant is a member and would be allowed to return to that country, if removed from Canada, or has a right to have the claim determined therein;

Subclause (2) of Clause 48.1 states:
(2) Notwithstanding paragraph (l)(a), a person is eligible to have a claim determined by the Refugee Division if, in the opinion of the adjudicator or the member of the Refugee Division considering the claim, the person has a credible basis for a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group or political opinion in the country that recognized the person as a Convention refugee.
1 think that clearly indicates that there is discretion on the part of the two officers who must agree. If one of them felt that there was a shred of doubt, a shred of fear on the part of that individual, then he or she is referred to a full hearing in front of the two-member independent refugee board in a nonadversarial fashion.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank the Minister for his answer. However, I respectfully submit that it confirms the point that I have tried to make. Subclause (2) quoted by the Minister-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to the motion on Canadian youth presented by my colleague, and I would like to read the motion now:
That this House condemns the Government for its abandonment of our youth and its failure to provide adequate support for their education and training or meaningful employment and job opportunities, both temporary and permanent.
Mr. Speaker, I think I share the opinion of the three previous speakers, including the Member who spoke for the Liberal Party, the Member who spoke for the NDP and the Minister from the Conservative front bench. It is unfortunately true that the subject of youth is not discussed often enough in the House of Commons.
The Minister mentioned that he had expected some questions, but 1 would like to say to the Minister that if no questions are being asked about the particular portfolio for which he is responsible, and I may remind him that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) appointed him to defend the interests of youth, it is up to him to raise the issue.
When a Minister says in the House that he is not getting any questions, instead of blaming the Opposition ... I mean, Opposition Members don't blame others for the fact that they don't ask any questions! Perhaps the Minister should look closer to home and ask himself whether enough is being done for people to sit up and take notice and show an interest in the issues.
Since 1984, I have had a chance to get more involved in issues concerning senior citizens. I would like to remind the Minister, and this is not meant as criticism, of the title, position, salary, and all the benefits involved. He was not appointed to defend free trade. He was not appointed to organize the conference on the Constitution. He was appointed to deal with youth issues on a daily basis. I think that is important, and I speak from my experience with senior citizens. Since the de-indexation of Old Age Security pensions, there has been considerable organizing among this group, and they have managed, in various ways, to force the House of Commons and the various legislatures to address the needs and

May 7, 1987
Supply
concerns of the elderly, an approach that has been taken very effectively by our farmers, chambers of commerce, business, small businesses, multinationals and the trade unions.
We simply must-and I deplore that it is the case in this Parliament or the previous Parliament, under the Conservatives, the Liberals, the New Democrats, it does not matter- admit that in the provincial Parliaments as well, regardless of the fact that the NDP, the PQ or the Liberals may have been in office, the sad fact is that the Elouse of Commons or the legislative assemblies devote precious little time to youths and do not show enough concern for them.
Perhaps the explanation lies in the fact that everyone is young, but at one time or another all of us are in transition from youth to middle age and beyond. This may be why I never fail to recall that when the Lion. Member for Shefford (Mr. Lapierre) was appointed he was then the youngest Minister ever, and the same thing can be said about the new Member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Charest) when he was appointed Minister of State for Youth. Next year it will be someone still younger, a never-ending process which makes us suspect that in every Parliament it is always more of the same. Someone will point out that, because it is expected of him or her, an opposition Member is going to rise and move a motion blaming the Government for failing to show concern for young people. The benches are still in the same place, only individual Members have switched sides, and history repeats itself.
I suggest that Hon. Members deserve a word of praise for keeping the debate on a non-partisan basis so far. I would like to tell the Minister that on the basis of statistical data, we could certainly congratulate one another and brag about all the young Canadians who have jobs and all our promising young executives, lawyers and professionals generally. In life, no matter the colour of the Government of the day, there are always young people who function well and progress in their careers; the fact that Parliament is filled with people who were young once and that businesses are managed by administrators who were young once is proof of that.
I suggest there have always been young people who succeed, others who experience difficulties, and still others who fail miserably.
I would like to tell the Minister that it is not a matter of paternalistic attitude. I must admit that there are people who helped me when I was young and I am most grateful to them. I realize now that they might have been somewhat paternalistic in their attitude, but with hindsight, I realize that what they were doing for me was vital. I suggest that the Minister of State for Youth (Mr. Charest), our colleagues in the House of Common and all responsible people should play a vigilant and active role in this regard.
The Minister has listed and identified a series of problems. I think that, since September 4, 1984, the Government can be held partly to blame. We have had two Ministers, including one who was a complete failure and who was demoted. The new Minister took over this portfolio under difficult circumstances. The Ministry was moved from under the jurisdiction
of the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie) to that of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard). All these structural changes clearly show again that, while the Government might claim that young people are a great asset, it does not know what to do with them.
The Government does not know under whom the Minister of State should come. Within two and a half years, he has been moved from one Department to another.
What matters is not under whose jurisdiction the Minister of State (Youth) should be, or which seat he should occupy in the House, but to have a person who has at heart the interests of young people and who is aware that his or her task is not going to be easy. The same applies to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) and the Minister of State for the Status of Women. These portfolios are not easy, so that the individuals who accept these responsibilities must work very hard every day, to increase the awareness of their colleagues who are responsible for promoting the interests of other groups in our society. You have the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), whose first responsibility at the Cabinet table is to make representations that are genuine representations made by farmers, that are meeting real needs. And the Minister of State (Youth) must ensure that in the course of each discussion, each budget preparation, each Throne Speech, each move, each legislation, youth priorities are included. He cannot rely on his other colleagues. Not because of a lack of competence or whatever, but simply because each one of them has his own responsibilities and youth must be defended, they must be defended more strenuously because of a tendency to forget them.
And when I refer to a tendency to forget, it is true that as the Minister suggests there may be a tendency to refer to them in the course of speeches, but in reality, in actual moves, they become less apparent in terms of action.
The Minister mentioned he identified the problem following studies that were commissioned. They have come to identify that the problem is caused by young people leaving school, the lack of education-the so-called school drop-outs.
I have a feeling they could have recognized that problem during their first year, because it is not new. Everyone knew about it. What people and I would like to hear-and I hope, I even am convinced the Minister will rise to tell us-is what concrete actions are taken. Not free trade that can create more jobs for more people and more people will have jobs, like Hygrade sausages. The more people eat them, the fresher they are, and the fresher they are, the more people eat them. What we want is specific concerns for that age group, the young in need.
Right now, when you look at newspaper reports, after those studies, half of the young transients attempted to commit suicide. This is serious. Even if they can boast of figures, 1,000 more jobs than last year were created, when we look at those headlines, the wording, the situations, there is no reason to be proud and it is dishonest to rejoice over achievements when there are still people in difficult situations.

According to an article on a study being carried out by the department of lowertown community health, thousands of young people, to survive, are involved in drug testing. Mir. Charest: Mr. Speaker, first of all, my compliments to the Hon. Member from Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart). He tends to be quite forthright in his comments here in the House, but from the tone of today's debate you would think there must be something in the air, since Members have been so moderate in their comments compared with what we have come to expect. I must say I am very pleased.
I would first like to say a few words about the Ministry of State for Youth to put the creation of this ministry into perspective.
The ministry was created on very short notice in January 1984, at a time when youth unemployment was particularly high following the recession.
The Minister's mandate was two fold. It included speaking for youth in Cabinet, although I don't think the Minister was alone in addressing this particular subject.
The second part of the Minister's mandate consisted in coordinating the federal Government's activities directed toward youth. A ministry of state tends to represent a particular sector of the economy or a particular group within our society. We have, for instance, the Ministry of State (Forestry) and the Ministry of State for Mining. There is the Ministry of State for Status of Women and the Ministry of State for Youth. A Ministry of State is by definition attached to a senior department, and in this case, it was, I believe, the Department of the Secretary of State, or at least initially. During International Youth Year, a special fund containing $20 million was created and the money distributed over a period of 18 months across Canada, and that was as it should be. After International Youth Year, this temporary program was terminated, as expected, and people were left with the impression, and some wanted to give that impression deliberately, that the ministry

had become an empty shell. The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that the Ministry of State for Youth still has the same function. It has always been a ministry of state and it always will, and I have never heard the NDP or the federal Liberals say that we intended to make the Ministry of State (Youth) into something else. If I am mistaken, I wish they would say so today, and I think Canadians should know.
That being said, in the spring of 1986, the Ministry of State for Youth was transferred to the Department of Employment and Immigration, making available all the resources we find within this major department with more than 27,000 employees. My responsibilities include, for instance, the Student Summer Employment Program. I am also responsible for reviewing occupational training programs with the provinces, all of which involves a budget of $145 million annually. So the Ministry of State for Youth has specific responsibilities.
On another subject, Mr. Speaker, I may recall the basic principles that apply to youth employment, and I am referring to labour market conditions and how these affect young workers. The first principle is, that when conditions on the labour market are good and the economy is in good shape, young people have jobs. When the economy declines or is in bad shape, young people are the first to be out of a job, and when the economy recovers, they are the last to be called back. The answer is therefore that if we want young people to be able to enter the labour market, the economy must be in good shape. And I think all Canadians will agree that this Government has been able to deliver the goods in this respect. More than any other group in society, youth is particularly sensitive to the state of the economy, and it is therefore extremely important to allow for this factor.
Second, in 1985 the Government introduced its job strategy which is a tremendous step forward in the way we tend to treat young people, in fact all Canadians, on the labour market.
The job strategy has three fundamental objectives, at least I consider them to be fundamental. First, the emphasis is on training, which has not always been the case in previous programs.
Second, we feel that job creation should be the result of a partnership approach. We must seek other partners if we want to create permanent jobs in our society, and that is why we have also involved the private sector in some of our programs, since after all, most jobs are created in the private sector. However, if we want to go further than that, we have to explain to the private sector that it should include a training element within the job environment, if we want Canada to remain competitive in the years to come.
Third, the job strategy focuses on the long-term unemployed, in recognition of the fact that the problems are greater in this group.
What we must understand today. . . When we were planning our strategies, as I mentioned earlier, we looked at what was happening in Canada. The Hon. Member from Montreal-Sainte-Marie said:	Job creation is another

problem. He is right, in that job creation was foremost in our minds when we decided to go ahead with our trade policy. Our reasoning was as follows: Canada is a country that exports and will create its wealth on the basis of the opportunities it has to do business on international markets. That is why we have embarked on negotiations with the Americans, and we are pursuing our initiative within the GATT system. That is how we see the situation. And having made that choice, we have to develop technologies to maintain our position on international markets. Third, we must develop labour market policies.
In 1987, the difference is that in Canada today, despite the present unemployment rate, we have jobs that cannot be filled because there are no qualified workers to fill them. All young people who will join the labour market in the coming years will need at least such analytic abilities and training as will enable them to remain in the labour force and change jobs-for indeed they will be expected to change jobs-and unless they do have such abilities the labour market will be closed to them, or they will simply have to accept unchallenging work.
The ultimate outcome of all this could very well be that many young people will be facing this kind of situation: employment opportunities might open up for them, but even then they would not be qualified simply because they lack the necessary basic training.
You referred to your generation or our generation and you say: We want the same opportunities. Indeed it is important to keep that in mind and make people understand that anyone belonging to the preceeding generations of the 1950s could quit school without a diploma and, in most cases, land a job in a country where, as a result of World War II, the economic growth was practically limitless until the 1970s. But the situation has changed drastically since then and today we have to come to grips with the new reality.
All such issues being considered, Mr. Speaker, we have to seek new approaches. The initial step has been taken: first identify the youth problem, which is the transition from school benches to labour market. That is the most urgent problem for this Government. Hopefully you will join us within the consensus we now see emerging in Canada. If that is the case, I would like him to say so clearly. This being said, we then turn back to the provinces and tell them: The education system should be enlarged, should be developped to provide more options.

If it is too easy for young people to drop out of school and find themselves in a situation where they will somehow manage to survive, we may sometimes be doing them a disservice. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise today to speak on this motion and to put forward the very impressive gains which the Government has made in addressing the needs of young Canadians. I must congratulate the Minister of State for Youth (Mr. Charest) for the job he is doing with this portfolio. Not only by virtue of his age does he have an acute understanding of the problems faced by young Canadians, but also by his own experience.
When speaking of the problems of young Canadians we too frequently tend to isolate them as specific to that group. In doing so we do a disservice to young Canadians because we proceed on a false assumption to adjust their problems. Are the problems faced by a 21-year old unemployed single Canadian that much different than those of a 31-year old single unemployed Canadian or a 41-year old single unemployed Canadian? I think that in some ways the situation of the 21-year old may be far more advantageous because with the passage of time an older worker's ability to gain a job is impaired. My point is simply that, as the Minister has stated, the problems of youth must be addressed within the total economic context of the management of the country.
When we speak of the need for responsible management of Canada's resources, full development of opportunities, and exploitation of our resources we are talking about increasing the wealth and Gross Domestic Product of the country. When we speak of the need for increased and enhanced trade with other countries we are talking about the need to contribute to this country's wealth and the need to create employment for older and younger Canadians. We are talking about increased employment opportunities generally.
Those who refuse to acknowledge that economic policies of general application do not have specific rewards for this sector of our society are incorrect. When a young person grows up in a family in which one or both parents are unemployed, the lack of stable employment, a good income, and opportunity for the parents results in less advantageous social and economic circumstances. That affects the ability of a young Canadian, upon reaching the age of 18 or 20, to make decisions to take full advantage of the opportunities presented to him.
The confidence of such a young Canadian is adversely affected. There can be no doubt about that. Psychologists have done a number of studies which clearly confirm that the socioeconomic circumstances in which young people grow up affect their level of ambition, the level of education ultimately achieved, and their aspirations.
When we speak of the national deficit we are not talking of something which is of no particular relevance to young Canadians. As the deficit grows the Government's ability to respond to the special needs of young Canadians decreases. Of that there can be no question. In order to implement specific programs for any group within our society we must have the resources to do so.

May 7, 1987
Supply
With one-quarter of the national Budget going to pay interest on the national debt, we do not have the ability to make the type of response which I am sure all Members want. The Government is making progress in the reduction of the deficit, which is not of recent origin. Nevertheless, in our efforts to address the problems of young Canadians we are moving aggressively to free up resources in order to be able to increase opportunities for young Canadians.
Similarly, when we speak of interest rates we are talking about improving the general economic performance in the country. It is with a stronger and more vibrant economy that young Canadians will find their niche, their opportunities, and the chance to make their own opportunities.
The general economic performance in the country is far better today than it was several years ago. There is no argument about the problem and the need to respond to it. The Government is doing something about it. There can be no serious argument on that either.
Some will say that statistics can be used in a thousand ways. Perhaps that is true, but today I will cite some statistics which clearly measure the success of our initiatives. Since the recession the average unemployment rate for young Canadians has dropped from 19.9 per cent in 1983 to 14.8 per cent in March, 1987. That is an improved situation for thousands and thousands of young Canadians. The decrease in the unemployment rate was possible because of the improved economic and management policies of the Government.
The Government has given young Canadians the opportunity to finance their educations, to put some money in the bank, and perhaps to initiate a business enterprise. We are contributing to their personal development and their level of self-confidence. Youth participation is increasing rapidly as a result.
There are three more young people per 100 in the labour market now than there were in 1982. The situation for students has also improved. In the summer of 1986, 906,000 students were employed compared to 840,000 in 1985 and
715,000	in 1982. The unemployment rate has dropped accordingly. The situation for in-school youth is particularly good. Since January 1985, the employment of in-school youth has increased by 107,000 which indicates that more students both desire employment while in school and successfully obtain it.
A wide range of programs has been implemented under the very able direction of the Minister of State for Youth. Challenge '87 is a sensible program which gives young Canadians the opportunity to gain training while they work during the summer. Not only do they get money in their pocket, they get experience. If anything has been made clear as a result of the changing labour market it is that people who wish to continue to work must be prepared to upgrade and change their skills in order to respond to the changing market needs.
The Government has placed Canada employment centres for students on campuses. On May 15 I had the pleasure of opening two such centres, one in Antigonish and one in Port Hawkesbury in my riding. Through discussions with counsellors in previous years I have learned that these centres are an invaluable contribution to assisting young Canadians find employment. We also have a co-op educational program, which combines theory with practical training aimed at the initiation of students into the world of work. That is a total commitment of close to $5 million.
To address the particular situation of native students, let me say that we have the Native Internship Program at the secondary and post-secondary levels with a total financial commitment in the area of $2.3 million. These are but some of the programs in place responding to the specific needs of young Canadians. There is also the Job Entry program which was brought in as part of the Canadian Job-Strategy program. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, from personal experience that that has resulted in considerable human benefit to my riding.
Many of my constituents have been out of work for a number of years after completion of their formal education. They are now at the point where for a number of reasons they cannot gain employment. The longer they are out of the workforce, the more difficult it is to gain employment. Our Government responded by implementing the Job Entry Program.
As part of that program, people who fall within this group are given training and counselling which included life skills. We take a person who may be demoralized and suffering from a lack of confidence, who knows very little about searching for employment, and we ask that person to participate in a program, for which he or she receives funding, whereby these weaknesses can be addressed for a period of months. As a result of this program there are people in my riding who have found employment. But for this program they would not have had that opportunity.
There are some very sensible and specialized programs to address the needs of young Canadians. The funding for the Challenge '87 program, which is a student employment program, approaches $200 million in 1987 despite the fact that our Government is suffering from rather severe financial pressure. I might add with some satisfaction that the resources under this program have been managed this year to reflect the needs of the regions of this country, the higher unemployment regions, where there is a greater need for this kind of funding. In some parts of southern Ontario, students can gain summer employment without the assistance of a program like this. In a riding such as mine, the incentives provided under the Challenge '87 program are a critically important part of the summer employment program. I congratulate the Minister for ensuring that the program is sensitive to the regional economies.

That is, of course, in keeping with the total Government commitment to enhance opportunities in Canada's regions. Some people say that the Government is totally committed to private sector funding on some theological, philosophical or ideological basis. Nothing could be further from the truth. We look at our partnership with the private sector very pragmatically. It is viewed as the means to achieve the most impressive results for young Canadians. We look at the private sector, and the partnership with it, as an opportunity to create two jobs instead of one. There is nothing ideological about it. It is our experience and our conclusion that the private sector must be involved if we are to maximize the benefits which can accrue to young Canadians.
All of this is taking place within the context of a national reconciliation and ongoing consultation with the responsible provincial Ministers. As all Hon. Members know, we have a situation in this country today where federal-provincial cooperation is far more positive than it has been in recent years. Of course, the recent Constitutional Accord of April 30 is clear evidence of what is possible within a confederation when we have a positive relationship among the Governments which make up that partnership. This kind of co-operation extends to all facets of governing and the winners are all Canadians.
When it comes to designing training programs that cooperation is essential. The federal Government wants and requires the assistance and advice of the provincial Governments. Often they know the labour market situation in their own province better than the federal Government. We want to bring together that expertise. We want the provinces to put in a share of the financial resources which are required. We want them to participate in the decision-making process. All will benefit as a result of this.
What about the students at university? We hear so much about the difficulty experienced by recent graduates in finding employment. That highlights the need for a greater emphasis on training. It is no longer good enough to go to university and receive a Bachelor of Arts degree. Students must be trained as well as educated. As I said earlier, one must be prepared to go through a number of changes in one's training. Training is something which is not restricted to only those in their twenties. Training is something which all of us must be open to consider if we wish to continue to participate in an ongoing way.
There are problems we face in terms of financial management of a country, for example, low interest rates, and there are tremendous problems faced by young Canadians. As our Government moves on its path to economic revitalization, it is moving to address the needs of Canada generally and, within this context, the needs of young Canadians. We cannot separate the special needs of young Canadians. A new plant in my riding will hire someone 20 years old, 30 years old or 40 years old. If a plant is put in a riding such as mine, the unemployment problems of. all Canadians will be addressed. Let us give an opportunity to young Canadians to go to work and they will solve a lot of the other problems for themselves.
