We must give them the opportunity to be self-supporting and to find their own way in our society.
In closing, I would once again like to congratulate the Minister of State for Youth for the exemplary contribution he is making as a member of the Government. In his travels across the country I am sure he has developed a tremendous rapport with young Canadians.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-YOUTH-EDUCATION AND EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad also to have the opportunity to address this Opposition day motion today. This motion talks of the Government's failure to provide adequate support for the education and learning and for meaningful employment and job opportunities, temporary and permanent, for the youth of today's Canada. In examining that question it would be wise to look first at the over-all situation of the youth of today's Canada.
They are in a position, shall we say, of following and following fairly closely, what futurist John Kettle calls the big generation, the post-war baby boom generation as it is also known. Therefore, they are in a situation quite unlike that of any other generation in history except, of course, in societies or areas devastated by war, disease or famine, in that they are outnumbered by their elders.
This leads, and has led, to some very unfortunate effects in all dimensions of social and economic participation by the young people of today's Canada, the people who we might loosely take as being in that age range from teen-age to the late twenties. Of course, these problems come at a time when problems strike the young person very hard, when lessons are learned, not necessarily either consciously or deliberately, but when the formative years of that person's adult life are being experienced.
I recall how, as one of the leading edge of the baby boom of post-war Britain, I went into a workforce that was not prepared for the massive influx that it was experiencing. Because of that sort of transition I myself experienced unemployment on more than one occasion for periods of some months. I can think back to how devastating that was in my experience. I wonder how it must be for someone today, looking at a situation in which they are not only unemployed but in which they cannot take any comfort from the thought that it is in some way inevitable that they will eventually gain employment, which was a notion I could take some comfort in simply by looking at the statistics. However, the statistics today are far worse. They are statistics to which the Government should pay some attention and with respect to which the Government should offer some remedies.
The situation that we have today, and I will go into more detail in a moment, regarding the unemployment of young people is pretty steep. The odds against the unemployed person getting that first job are high. Those who do so are fortunate and those who lose that first job often have difficulty in getting a second. Today, young people are also subjected to remedies,

May 7, 1987
Supply
to nostrums and to platitudes. It is in that context that I would particularly like to take exception to the remarks of the Minister.
I have the feeling that if the Minister really felt that he had a good word to spread, some good news to proclaim, then we would have had a lot more in terms of facts and figures and a lot less philosophy and examination of ideologies than we in fact heard from the Minister. While it is indeed a platitude that the youth of today's Canada are the future of Canada, nevertheless it is an idea that if we were ever to lose grasp of it, if we were ever to let go of it, we would be taking a very serious step in the wrong direction. 1 feel that it is inappropriate for the Minister to devote so much time and effort to condemning what he sees as platitudes. We acknowledge that they are platitudes, but God forbid that we should ever lose sight of the idea and of the priority which they encapsulate.
The youth of today's Canada are subjected to psychological pressures other than those I have mentioned. There shortcomings are being endlessly identified. They are, after all, treated by the media in the same manner as aircraft-we only hear about the ones that crash. Very few are offering them alternatives or, indeed, even offering to discuss the alternatives that the youth of today may see.
Unemployment among young people in Canada today is endemic. There are approximately 4.5 million Canadians between the ages of 15 and 24. Approximately 500,000 of those fall into the category of unemployed. That does not include some 20,000 or 30,000 who have stopped looking for work or the estimated 180,000 underemployed.
The Hon. Member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. O'Neil) suggested that the Government should take some credit for the reduction in the official, and I stress the word "official", youth unemployment figures from, I believe it was, 19.7 per cent to 14.3 per cent. However, the very preposition that he used in instancing those figures illustrates the falseness of their use as a claim for credit since, as he said, coming out of the recession-and those are the facts-we naturally expect that unemployment will fall. Unemployment has fallen over-all in Canada. It has certainly not fallen more for youth in percentage terms than it has for the over-all labour force. So, frankly, for the Government to make any claim of credit for a fall in youth unemployment is an illusion that would be even more dangerous if it really believed it.
The topic of discouraged youth is one which is of course very difficult to get a handle on, very difficult to get a grasp of; but there is a belief that there are large numbers of young people who are simply not reporting, in labour force terms. These are young people who have gone back to school or who have taken some other course of training or education, which they do not really have a commitment to, simply because they know that the prospects of getting a job are so poor.
I believe that if we were to add up those youth who are unemployed, underemployed, discouraged or, shall we say, misemployed, we might well find that one-third of Canada's
youth fall into that category. Yet what has the Government done? I am afraid that the answer is, precious little. To illustrate my point I will use some examples.
The Katimavik program was eliminated in February, 1986, and there has been nothing to replace it in the intervening 15 months. Some $1.5 billion was lost between 1986 and 1991 for post-secondary education. The budget of the Youth Ministry was eliminated. The funds for International Youth Year were also eliminated and no new funds were allocated for follow-up work. In terms of Challenge '87, some $30 million were set aside, in the sort of shell game that one cannot even run on the street any more, for the census, and the private sector orientation which, unfortunately, has led in many cases to employers simply covering with government dollars the training or additional hiring that they would have done from their own resources were the funds not available. Finally, the Canadian Jobs Strategy has been cut from $2.1 billion to $1.5 billion. The Canadian Jobs Strategy represents the investment that the country is making in terms of job development. It is an investment which, to a large degree, naturally, goes toward young people.
When we take into account the effects of inflation, we have seen the Government spend $3 on job creation for every $5 that was spent in 1984. That is not the sort of record that reflects credit. That is not the sort of record that will provide a hopeful future for today's youth.
We know-indeed it was raised in the House only yesterday-that young Canadians are discriminated against by the welfare systems in a number of provinces. Yet the Department of National Health and Welfare continues to pass funds on under the Canada Assistance Plan.
A statistic revealed just today is very telling in terms of the closing in, the shutting down, of opportunities for young Canadians. The following is a quote from a communique of the Public Service Commission of Canada dated with yesterday's date. It states:
The number of appointments of persons 24 years of age and younger decreased
from 1,836 in 1985 to 1,497.
That is a 20 per cent reduction in one year. Further on it
states:
The Public Service Commission considers this to be an area of significant
concern and is taking a hard look at its recruitment programs for qualified
young Canadians.
That is the picture we are getting in terms of federal government employment.
Katimavik is still unreplaced and the Challenge program is not upgraded to counteract the result of inflation, and indeed has been cut back during the Government's mandate.
Finally, to add insult to injury, there is the Hot-100 as it is called, "A quick guide to what the feds are doing for you". It could as well have been entitled "The federal program-Rag bag" because these programs are presented with absolutely no
May 7, 1987

attempt to target the audience or identify what programs might be relevant for an individual's requirements.
Let me give an example of how the programs are grouped. Listed in the Hot-100 is on-board service training with VIA Rail, as well as post-graduate education travelling programs to the People's Republic of China. That level of consistency typifies the efforts of the Government and the ministry.
If the objective had really been to produce publications and information systems that were useful to the youth of this country, the Government would have done it in a much more targeted fashion.
The New Democratic Party task force on youth was appointed in 1985 and travelled coast to coast. It released its report in February, 1986, and we believe that the youth prospects program as outlined by my colleague, the Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), would address many of the difficulties that today's youth face in Canada. In particular, we believe they would ease that transition from school to the world of employment that has been found to be so difficult. I know that many Members have spoken about the difficulties they experienced in that transition in the past. It is an important transition to which our effort should be applied.
The elimination of the youth Minister's budget was really a symptom of the problems the Government is failing to deal with in terms of programs to improve the employment and training opportunities for the youth of Canada. Much more serious is the cut-back in Established Programs Financing. Indeed, a news release by the Canadian Association of University Teachers states:
This legislation, if passed, will have the effect of restricting not only the
number of students but also the level of research that can be conducted by
university faculty. Universities will again become finishing schools for the rich.
That would be a terrible consequence if, in fact, that turned out to be the case. They state further on in the newsletter:
Post-secondary institutions, as every government study has shown, are in
financial crisis.
The Canadian Association of University Teachers very correctly point to the contrast between Canada and those societies which are putting more funding into post-secondary education, such as California and Japan. The percentage of GNP spent on post-secondary education declined from 1.35 per cent in 1977-78 to 1.24 per cent in 1985.
If the motives of social justice do not provoke concern about the quality of education in Canada, there is the clear message of superior economic performance that is being sacrificed on the altar of deficit reduction. Surely that should be something that the Progressive Conservative Government can understand.
In terms of the education and training components of the youth job prospects program which my colleague described earlier, our task force had a number of recommendations on post-secondary education. There should be stable funding, and funding increases should cover the cost increases. We should look at the possibility of returning to a 10-province standard and ensure the elimination of discriminatory practices against
Supply
international students. The Hon. Member for Grand Falls- White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) made some very telling points on the importance of that question.
The task force recommended an increase in both educational and employment opportunities by providing a longer term funding base and that tuition fees should be kept at approximately the current level. Most important, the task force recommends that the Government recognize the urgent need to provide all students in the secondary school system with both personal life skills and career counselling. Without that, the best system of education and training can produce less than superior results.
We placed a heavy emphasis on the importance of funding, particularly in smaller communities such as in my riding, of community organizations and non-profit organizations to provide services to youth and encourage the programs which increase the involvement and employment of young people in providing those services themselves.
Let me turn to the aboriginal youth, one group of young people in Canada in particular who are severely disadvantaged by the lack of involvement and support by the Government for programs designed to assist youth. They are part of a baby boom in this generation that occurred in the wider society in the last generation. Their numbers have led to an unprecedented crisis in the employment of young native people in this country, particularly on reserves.
Meanwhile, the Government has reduced job creation funds and redirected them to the private sector, which is generally almost absent on Indian reserve lands. To add insult to injury, the Government has cut out the housing labour component which used to be available from Canada Employment and Immigration Centres but is now absent under the Canadian Jobs Strategy.
This generation of aboriginal youth in Canada is the most highly educated ever. There has been almost a geometrical progression in the number who have taken advantage of postsecondary education and the funding assistance which is available to them as a treaty right for that education. We are faced with the unfortunate contrast of declining opportunities for employment, particularly in their home communities, with the burgeoning capacity of those native youth to handle the jobs and challenges that are available.
It appears that the Government has recently introduced a cap on the amount of funding that will be available for postsecondary education of native students. Indeed, some have been refused assistance. That was a regressive policy decision and one that was taken without an examination of the alternatives, except for the long term.
The alternatives for the short term should have been seriously considered and there should have been some consultation with national native organizations to ensure a degree of equity and understanding of what the Government's motives might be in making those cut-backs. That funding should be reinstated because the Government must have a policy of

May 7, 1987
Supply
investing in the education of native youth so that they can not only face the challenges and perform in the wider society, but also perform effectively as members and ultimately as leaders in their own communities.
There is no single solution to community-based Indian education, but each community must be given consideration in the design of an education program because the majority of those who pass through that education program will continue to live in the community in which they grew up.
It is in that context that I am scandalized and extremely worried about the direction of the Government when I see some of the examples that are brought to my attention. For example, a school that burned down still has not been replaced after eight years and the students are still in temporary classrooms and accommodations. For the difference of a few tens of thousands of dollars, the takeover of a native education program by the band will be held up, even though the band has emphasized that that was simply the front end and did not represent the continuing operational requirement.
As a whole, the motion speaks of the need for greater government commitment and support to the youth of the country. That need is nowhere more evident than in dealing with the challenges before our aboriginal youth.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to comment briefly on my colleague's speech and in the first place on the issue of our Indian people. I cannot let this day pass without mentioning and acknowledging that our young Indian and native people are facing special problems and that this Government recognizes the fact.

In the context of native youth, it is important to remind ourselves that to a certain extent the anticipated solutions centered around what was indicated in the Senate youth report as being first and foremost-the problem of self-government. When I assumed the portfolio of Minister of State for Youth, that was the context and the perspective in which the problems of native youth were set. That was the background. In that context we respected the constitutional process. We all know the outcome, and I think we all sincerely regret that that was the background upon which native youth problems were set.
We have now had the outcome of the constitutional conference. I have since met with native people and native representatives. In the consultative process we will deal with the problems facing native youth. We acknowledge that they are a special case. I want the Hon. Member to know that, and I want the House to know that our commitment to native youth is in that vein.
I should like to direct a couple of questions to the Hon. Member. Do the Hon. Member and his Party agree that the most important problem-and I think he has already said it; if
that is the case, perhaps he could re-emphasize it-facing young Canadian men and women today is the transition from school to work, particularly for young people who have not finished high school? Also, does the Hon. Member think and does his Party agree that provincial Governments should be involved in the attempt to design solutions and develop a consensus in Canada around these problems? Do they think that they should be included in that exercise or that at least there should be an attempt to include them in the elaboration of solutions?
All of this would take place, of course, in the spirit of respect we have for the constitutional balance and for the national reconciliation which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has been so successful in bringing forward.
I have another question for the Hon. Member, because the position of opposition Members on Katimavik has not always been clear. speechtext:
In the first place, Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the Minister for having given his support to our young native people. I think that under the circumstances, the future of our native youth is more jeopardized than that of any other group in Canada considering that the birth rate is much higher among native people than among average Canadians, considering also that in the context of self-determination and selfdirection or self-government as they like to say, but I think that relations between our youth and the authorities or the Government will improve. I hope that they will improve in the next few years and that this first generation of young native people will set those authority concepts in the context of native self-governing communities.
As for the questions which the Hon. Member directed to me on the transition between schooling and work, I am sure that the Minister has read the report published by our Party. Of course, we consider such a transition as the most important step in the maturation process of a young Canadian. Those are the reasons why we have advocated and described in our report a comprehensive and universal program to support such transition.

In so far as consulting provincial Governments is concerned, it is evident that in the design of programs it is necessary to do it within the context of Canada's federal society. If the Minister wants to be complimented on his efforts in this regard, I give it freely. I think it is entirely appropriate for him to do that.
In so far as Katimavik is concerned, my Party is not concerned that Katimavik be resurrected from the ashes as an article of faith. Rather, it is concerned that it was cancelled without any plans to replace it and without any indication from the Government about what were the deficiencies in
May 7, 1987

Katimavik which led to it being terminated. The program was simply abolished. We did not obtain a clear idea of why, nor did we get anything from the Government which could be seen as a replacement for Katimavik.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-YOUTH-EDUCATION AND EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, certainly it is a pleasure to have an opportunity to participate in the debate. When I heard of the motion of the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) last night, which referred to the abandonment of our youth and the Government's failure to provide meaningful employment and job opportunities, I could not believe that he was speaking about the Conservative Government. Therefore I called the Hon. Member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Charest) and said that I wanted to set the record straight.
The Hon. Member opposite and I shared a profession in education and a dedication to young people. Obviously we are seeing it from two different points of view today. From my point of view, our time in Government has been spent dealing with the issues faced by Canadian youth and showing a great deal of leadership. I will outline that in a few minutes.
I listened to the debate this morning and I could not help but wonder whether we were talking about youths or students in that there is a difference. When we are talking about the youth of Canada, we are not necessarily confining ourselves to students. As I am sure the Hon. Member knows full well, the studies have indicated-and he learned it as an educator many years ago-that 70 per cent of the young people about whom we did not talk this morning are the ones about whom we should be talking. Those 70 per cent who do not go on to receive post-secondary education become a very real factor in dealing with youth. That is compounded by the figures which show that on average, about 250,000 young people leave school each and every year. There are 250,000 youths every year with no kind of high school certification at all. That makes for a real problem and the Government has addressed that problem.
I would like to talk about some of the programs we have developed specifically to deal with the facts we found when we came into Government in 1984. The Canadian Jobs Strategy did not come about by accident. A lot of thinking was done about the problems faced by Canadian society and particularly young people. Several parts of that six-prong program are
Supply
specifically designed to address youth unemployment problems, and the successes of some of them are legendary.
I believe there has been some mention in this debate of the Job Entry Program. One of the significant parts of this program is the co-operative education program. The Hon. Member opposite should know that giving young people experience in the world of work while still in the formal part of their educational program is very significant and is a high priority. That is exactly what co-operative education has done and its effects have snowballed.
I can recall 10 years ago seeing very little co-operative education in Canadian schools. Now there is not one respectable school board or post-secondary institution that does not have a co-operative education program. Clearly the Government has played a lead in this, not just with talk but with money. The budget has increased in the years we have been in Government and rightly so. Money is well invested when it is invested in keeping young students on the right track, learning about the world of work, so they can enter that world and prosper.
Another feature of the Canadian Jobs Strategy is the Job Development Program and it too has been wonderful. It has helped employers design and develop jobs to fit the marketplace as it evolves, and at the same time has brought on stream young people who can learn the jobs as they develop. We are seeing all kinds of new vocations and we needed a program that would develop those new vocations as the working society changes.
These young people are very fortunate to have a program like Job Development in which to become involved so that they can learn while they are working and while they are young and so that they can be part of a whole new series of job classifications. Again, I think clear leadership has been shown on the part of the Government.
There is another series of programs with which I have had a lot of personal experience and I would like to share a bit of this experience with the Hon. Member opposite. Some of these programs have affected perhaps not his riding but certainly his province. The programs to which I refer have done very well in the Maritimes. These programs are generally classified under the title Innovations. Under the Canadian Jobs Strategy, Innovations provides the opportunity to develop new solutions to the problems we face. There are two or three such innovations about which I want to talk.
The innovation with which I am most familiar is the SelfHelp Centre for Canadian Youth which started in London, Ontario. It was a local solution brought about by people who care about young people. These people came forward and made a submission to the forward-thinking Government under the Innovations plan, had it approved and went to work with the young people of the community. They found out over the past year that young people came in rather large numbers to this centre located in a kiosk in a busy shopping mall. The centre allows them to assess themselves, their abilities and

May 7, 1987
Supply
capabilities in the work world, and to find out what they need to measure up. The centre provides help in resume writing and makes some young people realize that they should return to school for more training and development. The centre provides self-appraisal, something which is very important.
I daresay that as other Innovations programs have developed in other communities around Canada, we have found even more ways to help the youth. One program that has reached Newfoundland is the YMCA's Youth Enterprise Centre located next door to the Hon. Member in St. John's. There are eight such centres across the country established to help young people achieve self-employment by setting up their own businesses and subsequently creating spin-off employment for others. The concept of entrepreneurship and getting young people involved in small business is really what this country is all about. All economists and not simply those on the government side have said that the economic fabric of Canada and the jobs that will be created in the future will stem from small business. We are helping young people learn about this firsthand.
As the Hon. Member opposite knows, this is a kind of on-the-job education that many young people do not receive in the existing school systems. Once a youth enters the real hard world we all face, he needs these kinds of experiences. If the YMCA's Innovations program can provide that in St. John's, Newfoundland, and eight other centres in Canada, I say congratulations.
It does not stop there. These innovations are spreading across the country. Canadians are coming forward in large numbers from all areas of society wanting to help young people help themselves. The Youth Employment Skills Program, the Say Yes Program, was recently announced by the Minister in St. Catharines and has now spread to the West. I was in Winnipeg in March and I know this program has spread there. It is designed specifically to provide disadvantaged young people with a 12-week course in job-search techniques, work adjustment and academic upgrading and is followed by a series of job interviews arranged as a result of a supportive corporate network. All kinds of people from the private sector are getting involved and becoming part of the solution. Again, that is another step forward brought about by a far-reaching, far-thinking Government that developed a philosophically acceptable program like the Canadian Jobs Strategy.
There is always talk about the Challenge '87 program. Earlier in the debate I heard Hon. Members ask what we are doing in the way of summer employment for students. They asked what we are doing to get students on stream, thinking about careers and getting experience in their off-school time which, in the majority of cases, is the summer time. I think the summer employment program we have developed is getting close to being state of the art. It is very responsive to the needs that exist in the various communities across Canada and I think we should be recognized for that.
The fact that last year there were far more jobs in Toronto and southwestern Ontario where I am lucky enough to live
than there were students to fill them means that we do not need money from the Government. The private sector has clearly taken over by offering opportunities for young people to get on-the-spot experience. Let us not put money there, let us put money where it is needed.
The way the Minister has addressed regional disparities has been exemplary. The fact that there has been an allocation of 15 per cent more to the Maritimes is great because it is needed there. There must be opportunities for young people there and we have clearly taken that step.
As well, there are kids with tremendous learning difficulties and emotional instability problems. This group of people for whom it is hard to find work exists in our society as it does in every other society. I believe we have worked with them very well. Even our summer programs, for example the innovations in WOW, are outstanding. The Hon. Member knows these people have never been near a workplace before. They shudder, they do not have the inner strength to even know for sure whether they should be there or how to act. They need all kinds of support and development. This program supplies that, and 70 per cent of those people are gaining strength from that experience in the summer. They are not dropping out of school, they are returning as students and that is a tremendous track record. They are not going to be joining the street people. We do not want them there. We want them where they can learn and develop and be part of Canada as it becomes the leading nation of the 21st century. We are well on our way.
Where else do we see leadership? I cannot help but talk about a subject which is very dear to my heart, as I am sure it is to the Hon. Member opposite. He must have gone through this with these young people. Some of these people will get a high school graduation diploma but they want to get out and work with their hands. They want to contribute to society. Yet they need further training to reach certain skill levels and an apprenticeship program will give them that.
A lot has been said about how the apprenticeship program should be reviewed. 1 am sure the Hon. Member has heard it from his constituents as I have heard it from mine. The program needs a lot of changes because the nature of work is changing. The skills required are changing. So let us give credit where it is due and look at what this Government is doing about this very burning question which we hear from journeymen back home, who is going to replace me? They came to this country from other lands in the 1950s and 1960s thanks again to an initiative by a Conservative Government in 1957 which encouraged them. They came here and built our industry. Who is going to replace them? That is the big question.
Given the regional and educational differences in this country, the time for leadership is now. I am so happy to report that the Minister and our Government have set up a comprehensive review of apprenticeship training arrangements with the provinces and territories and we are committed to
May 7, 1987

producing for 1988 and 1989 a revamped set of arrangements relevant to the modern job market. That is quite a commitment. We are doing something about a major problem.
I want the Hon. Member opposite to know that our caucus committees are hard at work solving the problems dealing with the effectiveness of existing programs and whether they meet skill needs. How do we increase the participation of women, natives and visible minorities? We have all heard about interprovincial mobility. There is 20 per cent mobility in any constituency in any given year so we must have some system of knowing that the skill levels reached in one province or one area will be acceptable and useful in another. Again we should get plaudits for getting this done.
In the appropriate areas of responsibility, the federal, provincial and territorial Governments, the employer and apprentices themselves, are funding this training. It cannot be just the federal Government doing it. We want people to help themselves and we are starting to see that.
Clearly we are seeing federal leadership. People are starting to notice. The young people are feeling better about themselves. They know that through these programs, whether they be in school or anywhere else, they are going to get a feeling for the realities of the world of work. These programs will give them self-confidence and career direction.
The examples I gave earlier about the Job Entry and Job Development Programs are just some of the ways we are reaching out. There is just no question about that. Look at reports like this one, "Innovations help young people finish high school". It says: "If I were offered a job today I would turn it down. I want to first finish the program because I know in the long run I will get a better job." This is a young person speaking in St. John's, Newfoundland. That is how they feel about the programs and opportunities provided by this Government as it reaches out across this land, to every nook and cranny, to help young people.
I think the situation is very clear. We have met the challenge. We are not stopping. I have given a couple of examples of our leadership role and we are nowhere near finished. The Minister has to be applauded by all Members of this House for caring as he goes across Canada and listens to the young people and sets the direction we are going to follow in the future.
This Government, like some of its predecessors, has vision. The Hon. Member opposite should think a bit about this. A former Prime Minister stood in his place here and talked about the road to the North and what it would do for Canada. At that time very few people could really understand the impact of that statement. We look back now and say it opened up the North. Look what this Government is doing with its policy concerning not only Arctic sovereignty but to have people live and work in the North. Look at the opportunities that will arise when that ice-breaker makes its roadway to the North. When we move into the far North that even the Right Hon.

We heard yesterday from the mayors of large cities about all the interesting innovations they have for their young people to renew the cities and urban areas of Canada. I find that very interesting.
1 do not think that I, in southwestern Ontario, or the Member in Newfoundland, would find that kind of job satisfaction and life satisfaction with being Canadian. Perhaps there is something magical in the North. Perhaps some of the opportunities in the North will open up because of the bold move of the Government to be there, and to want to be there. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-YOUTH-EDUCATION AND EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a member of the Official Opposition, I am sometimes asked by my colleagues in the Government why it is that the Opposition is always criticizing. First, the Opposition criticizes because that is the role of the Opposition in a parliamentary system. Second, the Opposition has every responsibility to do so when the majority of the Canadian people no longer support the Government, according to the polls. Our 40 Members are undertaking to express the views and concerns of the Canadian people about their Government. Obviously, the people of Canada are not satisfied with the way in which the Government is conducting its affairs.
I must say it is our responsibility to remind the Government of what it has promised and that it has broken its promises. It is our duty to remind the Government where it has fallen short, where the people are dissatisfied and disillusioned, when people hurt and what their feelings are about the problems they face on a day-by-day basis. It is our duty to speak for the Canadian people. This is an Opposition day and for this reason-

-the subject matter before us today is as follows: consideration of an opposition motion:
That this House condemns the Government for its abandonment of our youth
and its failure to provide adequate support for their education and training or
meaningful employment and job opportunities, both temporary and
permanent.

That is our subject. It is about our young people. It is a subject which is probably the nearest and dearest to the hearts of the majority of Canadians, whether it is the young people themselves who are concerned about their own future or we as parents or grandparents. Therefore, let us ensure there is no mistake. Our young people are going through a very grave crisis right now. The Government does not seem to understand this and that explains why it is in such disarray and disfavour
Supply
with the Canadian people. I suggest that the Canadian people are concerned about their young people above all.
Half of our single young people, are living below the poverty level. Unemployment in the Atlantic regions is somewhere between 25 per cent and 30 per cent for our young people. In British Columbia it is about the same. If we can imagine, Mr. Speaker, that one out of four, one out of three, one out of four or one out of five in various parts of our country cannot find work, we can understand the rate of suicide has skyrocketed. In the face of this ethos of pessimism, the problems of unemployment and poverty, no wonder the young people have such a feeling of despair and hopelessness.
We are not talking in a hysterical way about the situation. We are talking about the plight of young Canadians. If only members of the Government would understand that we are talking about Bill, Bob, Mary and Martha-real people. When we talk about statistics, we are talking about real people. We must call the Government's attention to this issue of real people. It must wake up. It must be concerned, not about statistics but about these real people. There are real people living in poverty. There are real people, young people, lined up in the bread lines. Young people are living in poverty. Young people are unemployed and young people, in great numbers, are feeling very despondent. This is reality. We are not trying to dramatize anything. We are trying to make the Government understand that this is real.
We have heard various people from the Government side, and the Minister of State for Youth (Mr. Charest) as well, lecture us that it is important that in an age of technological and trade competition we need a well-educated society, that our young people must be well trained in the technological sciences and be able to be competitive. I could not agree more with the those observations. However, it seems strange how over and over again we find that the Government tells us one thing, then practises something totally opposite.
Having told us today how important post-secondary education and the new technology is, we learn that in fact the Government has decided to put a cap on the amount of money to be spent on our native Canadian young people who want post-secondary education. The Government is going to put a cap on that amount. It may be a cap the Government feels is high enough, but what about the commitment of all administrations in this country that native peoples, Indians and Inuit, will have the right to have post-secondary education, whether it be in community colleges, universities or whatever? There should be no cap on the amount of money for that, because there is no higher priority for this country in terms of obligation. The young people from those areas and those backgrounds must be unquestioned and unchallenged in their rights. But the Government has apparently decided to place a cap on the amount of money which will be spent on the postsecondary education of those young people.
The Government may have an answer for that, but there are other things which are inconsistent. For example, is it not strange that the Government and the Minister of State for

May 7, 1987
Supply
Youth and others have talked to us about the new challenge program for this summer. The Government is going to spend money advertising the importance of hiring young people this summer, the importance of private enterprise, and the fact that we must hire young people. That is a very laudable cause, but it is not very consistent with the way the Government carries out its own practices. We have just learned from the Deputy Minister that the number of Public Service appointments of people aged 24 years and under dropped to 1,497 down from 1,836 in the previous year. Barely four per cent of the 217,000 public servants are under 24 years of age. Imagine the Government lecturing us in this hypocritical fashion about its great concern for young people and cutting down on the young people serving in the Government.
At the same time the Government tells the private sector, "You should hire young people". This is hypocrisy. I know no other word for it. It is an incredibly hypocritical policy. How could the Government demand of the people of Canada that they should hire young people saying, "Do as I say, not as I do", while it cuts back the number of young people in our Public Service?
I would like to refer to something said by representatives of the Public Service Commission. They say that five years from now if the present trend continues we could have very few young people in the Public Service. That is hypocritical. Imagine the Government calling for others to hire young people when it does not do so it itself; when it is cutting down on the number of young people in its own service.
The next point I would like to make is that the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) pointed out in the House of Commons the other day that there was a grave problem of unemployment facing our young people. He asked a question of the Government. Quite rightly he was concerned about young people. He pointed out to the Government that the youth unemployment rate is up by 50 per cent in Manitoba this year as compared with 1980. He said that the rate was up 75 per cent in Saskatchewan, 81 per cent in British Columbia and 157 per cent in Alberta as compared to the figures for 1980.
What was the response when the Leader of the Opposition expressed his concern and said to the Government, "Please tell us what you are doing about this?" What response did he get from the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski)? He answered our Leader by saying that at the same time the youth unemployment rate has fallen from 18.3 per cent, nationally, to 14.8 per cent. Instead of dealing with the problem he told us that the rate has dropped. But dropped from what? He is comparing it with previous statistics of a few years ago in the depths of the recession. Instead of seeing that there is a problem and instead of admitting that in 1980 the situation for young people was very far better than it is today, the Government answered with statistics that tell us how much better it is now by, I think, 3.5 per cent than it was in the
depths of the recession. That is hardly the type of answer that will bring any type of satisfaction to Canadian people.
It is small wonder that the Government is in such disfavour with the people of Canada when they see that, indeed, statistics do not lie, but that liars can use statistics. This is not the type of answer of concern and feeling that should have come from the Deputy Prime Minister of Canada when asked about the grave difference in terms of employment between now and the beginning of this decade. At this rate throughout this decade there will be no hope. It is no wonder that there is a sense of despondency and hopelessness among so many young people. There are parts of this country where young people cannot really look forward to finding a job. Therefore they feel as if they are members of a lost generation.
When talking about youth unemployment we must remember that we are talking about human beings, individuals-our children. I am afraid that the Government has not appreciated the gravity of the situation. It has had a laissez-faire attitude, a simple slumping back and letting-things-happen approach. It thinks that if the whole situation with the economy improves statistically, then somehow that will trickle down to the young people. Instead of facing the problem and doing something in terms of programming and encouragement for our people the Government depends on a trickle down idea that somehow or other, eventually, if the economy of the country is good enough, everyone will come out all right.
We know that that is not the case. We know that while the economy is perhaps in good shape in the Golden Horseshoe, the area from which I come, and in certain parts of the country the opposite is the case. The west is hurting. It is hurting in terms of its farms, its energy industry and in so many other areas. The spinoff from the hurting in those areas also affects other industries as well. The west is in serious economic trouble. The same thing can be said about other parts of the country such as northern Ontario and the Atlantic region. So it is not good enough just to let things unwind, to let the universe unfold in that sense. It is important that the Government recognize its responsibilities and work actively on the subject of the problems that face our young people.
However, the Government has a record that is deplorable in this respect. It has closed down the Katimavik program, a program for young people that was achieving many things for them. After all, it was better than nothing. In fact, it was an excellent program. It was doing something for young people, something which the Government did not feel it needed. The Government closed down the First Chance program which worked to give young people the opportunity of finding that first job, after which they could then say, "I have experience", and then get another job and move on, to try to end the cycle of no job, no experience; no experience, no job.
The Government also closed 30 per cent of the employment centres on the campuses of the country. In other words, it cut out the vehicles for finding employment for young people as part of its program. That is hardly an enlightened approach to youth unemployment. It froze the student loan assistance
May 7, 1987

rates. The Government froze funds which were going to research councils which in turn would find their way to the universities and our young people. The Government cut back on the post-secondary educational funding formula. I could go on with a list of the tragic cut-backs that have faced research and students across the country in ever so many ways.
The other day I addressed a question to the Secretary of State of Canada (Mr. Crombie). I asked him why it was that the Government still has not set up a system to help the young people in the remote parts of our country where the unemployment situation is so high. I was referring to Newfoundland and British Columbia, for example. I asked why the Government had not set up a system which would allow students to repay their loans after they found a job instead of within six months of finishing school. The Secretary of State admitted that the Government was thinking about this approach. Ele said that the Government was studying it.
But the Government has not moved to help to alleviate the problems facing young people so that they will feel encouraged to go to university. They think now, as do their parents, that they cannot go to university or community college if it means that when they have made loans they will have to start paying them back six months after getting out of school, whether they have a job or not. What the Government needs to do is arrange it so that when a person goes to school they can have the confidence of knowing that they do not have to start paying back their loans until they get a job. The Minister agreed that that would be a good idea, but nothing has been done yet.
I then asked the Minister why the Government did not arrange that when students start to pay back this money it be related to their salaries. A person starting in a first job may start at a very low salary. I asked the Minister about having an arrangement whereby after a student is out of university or college, after having made a loan, that he or she would know that the loan would have to be paid back at a rate based on that first year's salary. This is something that frightens parents. They are frightened about getting themselves into debt. They are frightened about having their kids going to school and within six months of getting out having to put the money up front, whether they have a job or not, having to pay back the money at a rate of interest which is not related at all to salary.
That is another example of the lack of sensitivity that the Government shows to the plight of young people. The Secretary of State admitted when I put this point before him that, indeed, the Government was thinking about it, too. As a result of this debate we hope the Government will stop thinking and start acting.
In the area of post-secondary education we had a task force that travelled across the country to hear about the problems facing those in the post-secondary community. We concluded, with regret, that what we found across the country was a tragic situation. Reading from the text-
Supply

As a direct consequence of under-financing post-secondary educational and research institutions, teaching staff wages are frozen, facilities deteriorate, research activity is curtailed, morale is eroding, on-campus employment centers are closed down, foreign students are lost, scientists leave the country, libraries are undersupplied and laboratories become obsolete. Furthermore, post-secondary educational institutions are cornered into impossible choices to be made between accessibility and quality.
That is a brief summary of what we learned from 160 interviews with presidents of universities and community colleges throughout Canada, heads of faculty associations, members and leaders of student bodies including undergraduate, graduate and foreign students. The report was monochrome across the country, that the situation for postsecondary education is in crisis.
It is time for us to demand that the Government take steps now to face up to this situation and explore what it can do quickly and effectively to restore to our post-secondary educational community the quality which is required for our country.

I want to say that private enterprise is doing a very good job in this country. In my home province, in Quebec, it is thanks to private enterprise that young people could be saved. I ask the Hon. Member: Why always make taxpayers pay for everything in this country? The Government is always asked to pay. Why not let private enterprise take care of a few things? 1 have been

in the private sector for 20 years. I hired young people in the summer, I gave them work, I taught them a trade. Never did the Government give me a cent, and I did not want it either. I never even asked. But I can tell you one thing, I gave them training, and young people were very proud, at the end of school, to come work for me. Mr. Speaker, let me point out to the Hon. Member that I certainly have a great deal of faith in private enterprise. I am expressing a lack of faith in the Government, not private enterprise.
Perhaps the Hon. Member was not here when I began my speech. I pointed out that the role of the Opposition is, in fact, to speak on behalf of the people of Canada when they wish to express their dissatisfaction with the Government. Since some 75 per cent of the people of Canada are not supporting the Government and are critical of it, according to the polls, then our role is to try to speak on behalf of those 75 per cent. I suggest to him that many of those people who are critical, are dissatisfied with the plight of our young people today. I hope he will take that to heart.
Second, I was pointing out that the Government is hypocritical in asking private enterprise to hire more young people, as the Hon. Member did himself as an entrepreneur. That is great. However, the problem is that there is a state of "Don't do as 1 do, do as I say" when the Government admits that it has cut back on the number of young people it employs in the Public Service.
I have read the statistics into the record. They are not mine, but those given by Huguette Labelle who was using statistics from the Public Service itself. The projection from the Public Service is that the present direction of the Government will lead to a situation where "very few" young people will be working in the Public Service. Let the Government set the example.
The Government must also set the example as it applies to the handicapped and the disabled. We hear the same kind of double talk from the Government. We are told that 6 per cent of the people employed in the private sector describe themselves in some way or other as disabled or handicapped. We find that only 2 per cent in the Public Service describe themselves as disabled or handicapped. It is another case of "Don't do as I do, do as I say". The Government is not giving
as many opportunities for those who are disabled or handicapped as the private sector.
Indeed, I trust the private sector. I only wish that the Government would, itself, behave as well as the private sector.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my sense as we consider this debate today that there is a tremendous feeling of urgency with which we in the House of Commons should be addressing the problems of young Canadians. The latest unemployment statistics I have show that the unemployment rate for March was 17 per cent, up from 16 per cent in February and an increase from March of last year.
Would the Hon. Member for Eglinton-Lawrence (Mr. de Corneille) agree that in order to create a positive environment with respect to a future for our young people it is necessary to have a set of concrete proposals as opposed to a set of laments about the failures of the Government?
While I agree with those laments about the failure of the Government, do we not need to establish a youth initiatives fund to let young people practise some of that entrepreneurship which has been so praised? Do we not need to give guarantees to the educational system with respect to their basic funding, which was not given by the previous Government or the present Government, so that they can have some sense of security?
Do we not need some training initiatives tied closely to the private sector? Do we not need community initiative funds to give communities the possibility of creating long-term jobs for young people and providing young people with a future? Do we not have to talk about a complete reorientation of our economic policies so that we move toward expansion in our economy and away from constrictions which have marked Governments for the last eight years and have created unemployment rates that are humanly unacceptable both to young people and to society as a whole?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-YOUTH-EDUCATION AND EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, certainly at this point in time the Government has a very real responsibility to abandon its laissez-faire policy, that is, the trickle down theory that if the economy is doing well it will eventually reach everyone. It should realize that it is not reaching the young people and that strategies are needed to bring about a change in the situation of despair faced by young people. It is incomprehensible that in a country as wealthy as Canada we should have a situation where our young people are facing such stark hopelessness.
Those of us in the House of Commons with families must admit that we are not suffering too badly. However, I wish members of the Government would ensure that Cabinet understands-and they know what is taking place in their ridings-the impact upon young people, the unseen. They should be the voice of the voiceless, not cower in submission and accept this unacceptable policy of the Government.
May 7, 1987

We had a first chance proposal when we faced the electorate in the last election. In fact the Liberal Government had put the program into effect because we realized that we needed to ensure that the cycle of not being able to obtain a job without experience and vice versa had to be broken. We knew that something had to be done, that some positive, activist steps had to be taken, in order to break the cycle.
I call upon the Government to take this kind of step, to swallow its pride, or at least to have compassion and realize that a passive policy is no longer good enough. We have reached a crisis situation. Waiting for the economy to pick up to get these people employed is not working; something must be done.

Member for Eglinton- Lawrence, my Liberal colleague, was negative in the extreme. He criticized the Government's failure to act.
Mr. Speaker, I can inform the Hon. Member that when his party was in power, and the Hon. Member for Eglinton-[DOT] Lawrence was talking about compassion, he did nothing, absolutely nothing. He never rose in the House to defend our youth when unemployment rates were as high as 21.3 per cent. Where is his compassion? When he talks about hypocrisy, he ought to know what he is talking about. Mr. Speaker, just what is hypocrisy, morally speaking? It is when the Hon. Member rises in his seat and claims that this Government, that our Minister of State for Youth (Mr. Charest), and never mind that they introduce programs that work, programs that give young people a chance to do something else than paint fences, programs that prove that Canadian young people are not a kind of disease that has to be isolated but a group that should be integrated in society and given its fair share and a chance to show what it can do. Tomorrow, they will be the decision-makers and not those hypocritical critics, Mr. Speaker, who are saying sort of virtuously that the Government did nothing.
Mr. Speaker, during the twenty years they were in power, they forgot to help Canadian youth. They abandoned youth, Mr. Speaker. All the departments did.
Today, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Eglinton- Lawrence rose to preach a sermon on charity and what our youth policy should be. We have a Minister of Youth who had the courage to rise in his seat today to ask the Opposition whether it had any contribution, any solutions to offer. He said
Supply
it would be a pleasure to work together with the Opposition. That was unheard of under the Liberals. They thrived on arrogance and refused to listen to the provinces and the Opposition parties. Bad mouthing their neighbour, that is what they were doing, including the Hon. Member for Eglinton- Lawrence.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot accept that in the name of Canadian youth, a Member such as the Hon. Member for Eglinton- Lawrence play small party politics. Mr. Speaker, when we look at the programs, I did not hear him say once that we put in place Challenge '85, '86, '87, we put in place the new Job Development Program, we put the accent on training, because it would be unthinkable for a responsible Government, a Progressive Conservative Government, not to provide training under our programs. It would be unthinkable, Mr. Speaker, to let the young wallow around the place in the hope that some day or other something will happen, there will be a breakthrough somewhere.
Mr. Speaker, we took our responsibilities, and when I hear the Opposition, when I hear the New Democrats suggest the Minister of State for Youth did not do this or that, I find it very hard to accept that they can use such terms, because youth does not merely involve the Minister of State for Youth. It involves all Canadians. It is also the responsibility of each Department. We can see that in the area employment and immigration, we can see that in the area of regional industrial expansion, thanks to lower interest rates that allow the young to start in business, thanks to small business loans at affordable rates. We could ask them where the interest rates were when they were in Government, when home mortgage rates went up to 22 percent, when Canadian people lost their homes, when they could not build to make the Canada of today and the Canada of tomorrow.
And they now dare accuse us of doing nothing for the young! The young also involve the Department of Agriculture. Stable interest rates, long-term dairy policies, capital gains exemption that enables young people to start up in farming, to integrate into the Canadian farming system, because there is in Ottawa a responsible Government that offers them alternatives, that gives them a chance to get involved rather than suggesting: We will put you on hold, wait for you to get older and if we are given the chance to do so, we will make room for you.
Canadian young people are following this debate today in the House of Commons and considering alternatives. The Minister of State for Youth has put forward some alternatives within the context of existing programs that were established in 1984. They asked opposition Members whether they had anything to say and they answered no, we have not. They said, to use the clever words of the Hon. Member for Eglington- Lawrence, that they are here to criticize the Government because that is the duty of the Opposition. That shows, Mr. Speaker, how mature opposition Members are.

May 7, 1987
Adjournment Debate
Mr. Speaker, that I cannot understand and to conclude, because I know that time is running out, I want to say that a responsible Government is one that makes room for its youth, that says to young people: You are going to get involved, we will give you the tools, we will not do as the Opposition, we will not spoon-feed you in the belief that what we are doing is good for you. We will provide you with the opportunity to be yourselves, to become adults, and to ensure that tomorrow's Canada is the one that you have chosen and not what we have tried to impose upon you.

subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-TESTS FOR ADMISSION AND SELECTION OF PERSONNEL-GOVERNMENT POSITION (B) OFFICIAL LANGUAGES-REQUEST THAT SOLICITOR GENERAL PRESENT REPORT

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-TESTS FOR ADMISSION AND SELECTION OF PERSONNEL-GOVERNMENT POSITION (B) OFFICIAL LANGUAGES-REQUEST THAT SOLICITOR GENERAL PRESENT REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, again this evening I should like to raise certain questions which were asked in the House concerning official languages and which have yet to be answered.
As recently as May 5, two days ago, I asked the Solicitor General if he could do something to correct a situation within the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, a situation related to the RCMP aptitude tests which have been shown to be discriminatory towards francophones because the test translated from English was full of errors. As a result of these errors, successful francophone applicants had an average of 60 per cent, whereas the anglophone applicants' average was 70 per cent. So the RCMP hired more anglophones because francophones found it difficult to pass this selection test.
Admittedly, Mr. Speaker, this may have been due to an erroneous translation, but they kept the test and used it for five years. Since 1981 they knew the test was incorrect but they kept using it anyway, and RCMP officers themselves had to complain publicly before corrective measures were taken.
Mr. Speaker, this is not the first time in this House and in the Standing Committee on Official Languages that I single out some of the anomalies-and I am being polite-which exist within certain Government services. Faced with the RCMP inertia in taking action and responding satisfactorily to questions put to them, the day before yesterday, following the answer of the Solicitor General, I decided to write a personal letter to the Prime Minister, a letter which I sent to him and which, I hope, he has received and will answer. This letter, Mr. Speaker, is a summary of events since last fall with respect to official languages. I should like to remind the House that what I am saying now I consider as being very serious.
Last October 16 I asked a question in the House as a result of the publication of a document called Pony Express, a RCMP internal document. It was indicated in this document that they intended to reduce the 20 per cent francophone personnel quota to 14 per cent. Answering in the House, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) assured me that this was not Government policy. I believed him.
On October 23, again in the House, I made public the contents of a letter confirming this agreement between the RCMP Commissioner and the Treasury Board official responsible for implementing the official languages policy. Mr. de Cotret, the Minister, responded by saying that it was only a discussion among officials, not a Government decision. Again I believed him.
On Wednesday, December 17, 1986, in the official languages committee, RCMP Commissioner Simmonds confirmed the objective had been lowered from its level of 20 per cent to 14 per cent. He said it might be 12 per cent. The next day, I pursued the matter in the House and asked if it was the RCMP Commissioner or the President of the Treasury Board who was telling the truth and which of them we should believe. About the situation, the Minister replied to me that on October 2, the day before, he had requested the Solicitor General of Canada to present him with an action plan on official languages for the RCMP. And I believed him, Mr. Speaker. I said to myself: "There will be action, the Minister told me there will be a plan. It seems as if the Solicitor General is facing a de facto situation. The RCMP will have to act." I thought things would change. Nothing changed. On January 30, French-speaking RCMP officers publicly denounced the conditions they were in. Even the Deputy Commissioner of the RCMP Quebec Division, Mr. J. Julien, was critical. He wrote in a long letter to Commissioner Simmonds that among the French-speaking officers in his division, and I quote:
The feeling expressed is one of rejection of Francophones by the Anglophone
majority and that Francophones' participation in the RCMP is marginal.
It is upsetting.
I questioned the Government twice, on January 30 and February 2. Ministers procrastinated and refused to answer my questions. Then, on February 3, the RCMP appeared before the committee where Mr. Julien confirmed the authenticity of his letter and comments. The RCMP high officials who were present closed ranks and refused to budge on anything.
Faced with all these delays and this ghastly situation, the Solicitor General does nothing. I was rather disappointed the day before yesterday and I told the Minister: If you cannot do your job and enforce the law which has been with us for at least 18 years, resign!
May 7, 1987

Last Wednesday, before a parliamentary committee, the Director of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service confessed quite candidly, probably knowing full well that he did not have to hear the consequences of his action, that his organization had never met the requirements of the Official Languages Act in two years, that is ever since its establishment. This also falls under the jurisdiction of the Solicitor General, Mr. Speaker. Both the RCMP and the Canadian Security Intelligence Service do, Mr. Speaker, and nothing is being done.
Yesterday, or the day before, I was told: There is a report forthcoming. I asked the Minister who told me: Yes, I have received and tabled the plan with the Treasury Board. I will act on these matters next week. Tonight, I ask the Parliamentary Secretary to confirm whether we can hope for any corrective action, urge the Government to do something and suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if the Minister is unable to act, he should be replaced with his Parliamentary Secretary. I know he would do something.
