speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) is much too kind. First of all, I must say he has raised a major issue, namely the linguistic duality within Canada and our institutions. I want to congratulate the Standing Committee on Official Languages which, over the past few months, has really tried to remedy the situation, shaking the tree to get rid of the bad apples.
Of course, as minister responsible for the Canadian Security Intelligence Service and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Kelleher), knows just how important the French issue is within these two services. To raise it as radically as the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier did might be somewhat premature, because one should look at the context as it is, and as the Hon. Member for Ottawa- Vanier and you, Mr. Speaker, know it has not occurred overnight. If the Commissioner of the RCMP and the Director of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service have felt the need and taken it upon themselves to hire more Anglophones than Francophones, it is because there was something basically wrong which had not been detected and which has been coming to light over the past few months thanks to the tremendous efforts of the Official Languages Committee.
Mr. Speaker, it is a series of facts and circumstances which is coming to light from day to day and which explains why the Solicitor General is truly concerned with the problems resulting from the French fact. To get to a solution, I am sure, because linguistic duality, the French fact, is and always will be entirely acceptable within the Canadian system, is and always will be worth fighting for within our institutions, as the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier and French-speaking members of this House have always done. We must protect bilingualism. The Solicitor General will do so as much as he can and-something that should please the Hon. Member for
Adjournment Debate
Ottawa-Vanier-will always maintain a required decent minimum within our agencies.
I also commit myself to support my colleague from Ottawa-Vanier as well as all Members of this House as a democrat, as a Member respectful of Canadian laws, of both our languages, of both our founding peoples who will always be protected. I can assure the Hon. Member that the Solicitor General is well aware of the situation and will act as quickly as possible, even though he has already done so in several cases.

subtopic: CANADA POST CORPORATION-DELAYS IN MAIL DELIVERY
CANADA POST CORPORATION-DELAYS IN MAIL DELIVERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 20, 1987, in this House I asked the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre), who is also responsible for Canada Post, a question related to frustrations experienced by some of my constituents in dealing with the mail service. The Minister acknowledged the existence of problems and assured me that he is committed to finding some solutions.
I would like to praise the Minister for being very active in the past in seeking constructive and innovative measures in dealing with the situation, such as the appointment of a group to study the feasibility of third-party regulation.
More than anything, though, I strongly support the message conveyed through the Minister's actions that good service and not the reduction of the deficit should be the first priority of Canada Post. Considering the April 1 rate increase as well as the seemingly annual threat of yet another postal strike, I would like to make some comments on the matter.
I cannot stress strongly enough the important role that the Post Office plays in our lives. In my duties as a Member of Parliament I have dealt with problems experienced by Canadians with a variety of services such as those offered by financial institutions. As important as these are, the issues involved are often abstract and remote to most people. Service provided by the Post Office, however, is essential, tangible, and affects all of us in our most basic daily routine.
There are three groups of users of the Post Office on which I would like to concentrate. One is ordinary citizens involved in personal correspondence, the second is religious and charitable organizations, and the last is various business groups. During my term in office I have received hundreds of letters of complaints about personal mail delivery and only one-yes, one-complimenting Canada Post. Granted, Mr. Speaker, this is not a very scientific survey, but common sense suggests that there is something wrong. What is wrong?
According to the Marchment committee, which did a study for the Government last year, the most serious tangible problem is delay of service. Many of my constituents complain

May 7, 1987
Adjournment Debate
that there is no predictable time of day when the mail arrives and, at times, there is none for consecutive days.
The second group of immediate concern to me includes various religious and charitable organizations which require low-cost and efficient mail service to distribute their material. Two publications of the Canadian Church Press, namely The Presbyterian Record and The Canada Lutheran, have been denied second-class postal permits which are absolutely essential for their continued existence. The ground for this decision is that these periodicals are business and not religious. Mr. Speaker, if a church magazine is not religious, what is?
The subject of postal needs brings us to the third group affected by the Canada Post policies. Personal mail is important but it only constitutes about 8 per cent of the entire volume. By comparison, the lack of adequate service and the ever-increasing cost of mail service has a real negative impact on businesses, particularly small businesses.
To help put things into perspective, first-class business mail constituted about 4 billion pieces out of the total of 7.7 billion pieces handled by Canada Post last year. It contained various bills, invoices, tax slips, insurance documents, et cetera, which, given the obvious existence of deadlines and due dates, depend upon reliability of delivery within a reasonable period of time.
At the risk of sounding drastic, Mr. Speaker, promptness in such cases is a major factor in sustaining the economy and certainly the well-being and cash flow of enterprises involved. This is especially true of businesses which operate on performance margins directly related to postal rates.
Therefore, considering the volume of mail involved, even slight rate increases such as the one last month have a significant effect on profit margins. Furthermore, the lack of confidence has prompted many businesses to contact independent couriers for important pieces of mail, something which is an obvious additional burden on the costs.
I am strongly opposed to any rate increase without significant improvement in service, but I also realize that this is done because of the other major problems affecting Canada Post, poor productivity and the resulting deficit. For this the blame should be shared by labour and management. To begin with, the entire negotiating structure seems ridiculous in that there are eight unions and thirty bargaining units within the corporation. Not only does this prevent cohesive and coordinated bargaining but considering that unions tend to honour strikes across the country, one deadlock threatens to paralyse the entire system.
Given this, it would be instructive to look at some of the existing contractual provisions. For instance, in the letter carriers' agreement, full-time employees have the first right of refusal in replacing their colleagues who are absent on vacation or through illness. This means that a letter carrier who has completed his or her own shift, which incidentally can often be completed in three or four hours, has the option to
pick up his absent colleague's bag. This he will almost invariably do since one of the catches is that substitutes are paid time and a half. Considering that the contract prohibits hiring casual or part-time workers at straight time, there is an obvious incentive to maximize frequency of absence and diminish productivity.
Statistics strongly back up this notion. Last year the nonvacation absenteeism of Canada Post employees was 16.5 days per year, all paid according to contract. By comparison, the average for the rest of the economy, including truly hazardous jobs such as mining and steel manufacturing, was six days.
There is no doubt that part of the blame in this case should be attributed to management, which conceded irresponsible benefits during the last settlement. On the whole, the bargaining climate between unions and management is adversarial to the point of irrational spite. Labour, in particular, tends to assume an "us versus them" attitude and politicize any disagreements.
Obviously, in the short time I have I cannot say all that is wrong with Canada Post, nor can I provide the solution. However, I can offer some ideas. First, I believe that strikes affecting postal service are indefensible. Therefore, I have drafted a Private Member's Motion calling on the Government to make Canada Post an essential public service, thus prohibiting strikes. Aside from assuring Canadians that at least some service will always be available, this should help pre-empt in the future the kind of ridiculous concessions described earlier.
Naturally this is not a solution but only a small step. Beyond it, the entire negotiating atmosphere must be improved and de-politicized. In that sense, the Minister's initiative of setting up a team to study the possibility of a neutral non-government group involvement is a worthy idea. As for improvements in productivity under existing contracts, commitments announced in last fall's corporate plan, such as specific time targets for delivery, are constructive.
I would like to stress that the situation is nothing short of shameful and frustrating but not irreversible given our resources and know-how. Therefore, a commitment to improvement of service should be the number one priority of Canada Post in the immediate future.

Mlrs. Gabrielle Bertrand (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs): Mr. Speaker, I will try to respond to the concerns of my colleague and to those of all Canadian citizens.
Perhaps the single most important aspect of Canada Post delivery service is reliability, in other words the regularity with which the flood of mail is forwarded from the pick up point to the point of delivery.
In-depth market surveys indicate that postal service customers want to know how long it takes for first class mail to reach its destination.
May 7, 1987

The findings of the Marchment task force confirm those of the corporation.
All studies made suggest that postal service users are prepared to accept the following norms, provided they are guaranteed reliable service: two (2) days for delivery within the same city; three (3) days for delivery between major urban centres in the same province; and four (4) days for delivery between major urban centres in various provinces, that is from coast to coast in Canada.
The Corporation has set up a national control centre, which operates 24 hours a day, seven days a week, to monitor the efficiency of Canada Post by studying every step in the processing of mail, in accordance with the management plan of the Corporation. Canada Post has been introducing, since August 1986, a new color code. This system will enable managers of regional services to exercise a better control on our commitments. Each day of the week has been assigned a separate color and that allows the staff to determine precisely the priorities for processing and delivery.
The Corporation tries to meet its commitments related to processing and delivery of mail. It also emphasize the so-called "return program ". This is a program designed to correct mistakes due to a combination of factors, particularly errors in the postal code used by the sender, employees' mistakes and machine malfunctions. Canada Post has also bought 9,600 extra wire containers for intermodal railway service or for loading and unloading trucks carrying bulk mail, as well as
160,000	letter plastic containers for the safe transportation of mail.
The Corporation has a strategy which makes possible the sorting of all first class mail in 24 hours. That strategy is designed to make optimal use of facilities and machines, by distributing accumulated mail in order to reduce the number of items at rush hours and to increase it during slack periods.
To sum up, the facilities used by the Corporation and its network of means of transportation are being reorganized in order to process increasing amounts of mail on a more reliable and better monitored basis, through better management and a better use of equipment.

Mr. Speaker, on April 8 in the House I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) if he could advise me what progress he and the Government were making in terms of implementing social and educational initiatives to deal with child sexual abuse. These initiatives had been announced last year and, of course, we are urgently seeking their implementation. We are aware that the problem of sexual abuse of children is an extremely serious one. In fact, it has been estimated that four out of ten females and one out of ten males has been sexually abused before reaching the age of 18.
Adjournment Debate
I have been very pleased to be part of the legislative committee that dealt with Bill C-15 which sets out the legal framework dealing with child sexual abuse, which establishes new offences and penalties and which deals with the ability of children to testify in court. I hope that that Bill will very soon receive third reading and be enacted.
In addition to the legal framework, the Government has promised to take action in other areas as well. It has indicated that it will appoint a special adviser on child sexual abuse. This adviser would have responsibilities to deal with the social and educational issues. He or she would be supported by a committee of regional advisers who would seek out and bring forward ideas and input from the various regions of the country, as well as being representative of the many disciplines which have a strong interest and concern about this issue. I understand that this adviser has not yet been appointed. I urge the Minister and the Government to work as quickly as possible in this respect because I believe that this program needs the leadership which the adviser will be able to bring to it.
At the same time, the Government has also committed $20 million over a period of five years to focus national efforts on combating child sexual abuse. This complements other initiatives. In allocating these funds, I think it is important that the federal Government work closely with the provinces and non-governmental organizations in this effort.
I was pleased to hear that on April 14 the Minister of National Health and Welfare announced approval of $1.3 million in project funding as the first step of this five-year program. He also indicated that there were an additional 65 projects totalling about $3.3 million which were under consideration for the 1987-88 fiscal year. I was particularly pleased to see that of the $1.3 million in projects that were announced, about $350,000 in projects would be going to organizations in British Columbia that have played a leadership role in this field. Indeed, the question of child sexual abuse has been an urgent topic for the school system in British Columbia.
I want to comment on one specific initiative that is being undertaken by the British Columbia School Trustees Association. More than a year ago the association established a task force to advise the provincial Government and school boards on the question of child sexual abuse. Last fall they released an excellent report which deals with this issue in a forward moving and comprehensive manner. This report contained a number of concrete proposals for the provincial ministry of education.
Building on the experience gained from this exercise, and with project funding from Health and Welfare Canada, the British Columbia School Trustees Association will be sponsoring a meeting of national educational associations representing parents, teachers, administrators, trustees and provincial

May 7, 1987
Adjournment Debate
government officials to share information and develop goals concerning child sexual abuse.
I think the school systems of Canada are in an excellent position to effectively respond to the problem of child sexual abuse.
In the short term, efforts can be focused on prevention and raising community awareness of the problem. In the long term, our school system can educate the next generation against interpersonal relationships which encourage child abuse. Our schools can implement programs and follow up with research to ascertain the effectiveness of these programs.
By bringing together concerned parties from right across Canada, the forum organized by the British Columbia School Trustees Association can be likened to a springboard, to help develop a national strategy to deal with this very tragic problem.
This meeting, which is to be funded by the federal Government, will allow the participants to develop a comprehensive role for school systems of Canada which will facilitate implementation of programs at both the local and provincial level. It will help put in place an information sharing process, allowing for communication about the effectiveness of techniques to combat this ill and about the results of research.
It may also lead to joint projects among various jurisdictions so that the lessons learned from a program in one part of Canada can be applied to the efforts of another.
I applaud this initiative for it sets the groundwork for a coordination of efforts on a national scale in Canadian schools. I trust that the Minister of National Health and Welfare will continue to approve funding for worth-while projects such as this which complement the legislation introduced by his colleague, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn), and will finally, I hope, start to deal with the root problems that are involved in the issue of child sexual abuse.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Gabrielle Bertrand (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I want to congratulate the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) for her dedication to such an important problem as child sexual abuse. I can see that she is very well informed on the subject and I wonder if she does not already know all the answers that the Department or myself would like to give her.
Mr. Speaker, in June 1986, the Government announced what steps it intended to take as a follow up to the recommendations of the Badgley Report dealing with sexual abuse of
children and also those of the Fraser Report dealing with pornography and prostitution.
In addition to the changes to the Criminal Code and the Canada Evidence Act which are presently being contemplated, the Government has announced a social and educational program which is to be implemented through the Department of Health and Welfare.
However, the Government has fully recognized that under the Constitution the provinces are responsible for health services and social services in Canada. As part of its strategy, the Government has also appointed a special advisor on childhood who will be reporting directly to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp).
This special advisor shall be assisted by a committe of regional advisors which will promote the exchange of ideas between the various regions of the country and act as a forum for the numerous disciplines involved in the field.
It is expected that the special advisor shall be named shortly.
It is essential that the government appoint the best qualified individual and that no other obligation will prevent that person from taking up that position.
In June last, an announcement was made that the Department of National Health and Welfare will spend $20 million during the next five years to implement social and educational measures in order to provide guidance and define the objective of the national strategy to control sexual violence against children. In order to develop a program making the best use of funds in accordance with the government's commitment, the Department has undertaken consultations with provincial officials and non-governmental organizations. According to the Department, it would not have been worthwhile to develop that program too soon without having sufficient outside input, especially those of individuals and organizations which are primarily responsible for the provision of those services.
Therefore, the Government remains committed to support effectively that important program and it will reconsider responses at governmental level to the problems of sexual abuse of children as the program evolves.
